# Precompile

> Construct your Types when you build

# Overview

> Compile your Types when you build, and ship only the checks they need.

ArkType runs in two modes. Both take the same definitions and infer the same types.

- **Dynamic**: `type()` parses each definition at runtime and compiles it the first time your program uses it. No build step.
- **Precompiled**: [`@ark/aot`](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/tree/main/ark/aot) constructs your Types when you build. Each becomes a standalone validator that imports only `arktype/runtime`, so arktype's parser never ships and no code is generated at runtime.

```ts
import { precompile } from "@ark/aot/unplugin"

export default {
	plugins: [precompile.vite()]
}
```

[Setup](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup) covers every bundler, test runner and Next.

A precompiled validator accepts and rejects what the Type it replaces does, with the same error messages. The cost is a build step. [Every error it reports names its fix](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile#with-agents), so an agent can run it.

## Speed and size

A validator that compiles at runtime ships its compiler, and one that interprets ships its interpreter. A precompiled build ships neither: only the checks your Types need, and the runtime that reports their errors. Build the fastest validator or the smallest from the same definitions. The [options](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options) decide which.

**Runtime** (instructions per call, lower is better): moltar's parseSafe benchmark (validate, removing undeclared keys), run by us on Node 24, ArkType precompiled with the default options. Precompiled ArkType isn't in moltar's published results yet. Source: [moltar/typescript-runtime-type-benchmarks](https://github.com/moltar/typescript-runtime-type-benchmarks)

- ArkType (precompiled): 184
- ArkType (dynamic): 200
- Typia: 213
- ata-validator (AOT): 220
- @sx3/gate: 233

**Bundle size** (bytes gzipped, lower is better): the login form as valibot.dev writes it, with its messages, bundled by us with bundlejs's esbuild settings; each reports an error for every invalid field. ArkType is precompiled with its default options in a production build. Zod Mini's form is written so it runs: as valibot.dev writes it, it throws at its first parse. Source: [the form from valibot.dev's comparison](https://valibot.dev/guides/comparison/)

- ArkType (precompiled): 917
- Valibot: 1,564
- Zod Mini: 5,124
- Zod: 25,076
- ArkType (dynamic): 98,064

In our runs of moltar's benchmark, precompiled ArkType is the fastest on parseSafe and assertLoose. Precompiled with its defaults, it reports an error for every invalid field of Valibot's own login form, with the form's messages, in a smaller bundle than Valibot. Each chart names its benchmark and the options ArkType was built with.

A precompiled Type costs nothing to create: it was built when you built. Since nothing is generated at runtime, it runs under a Content-Security-Policy that blocks `eval`.

## Optimized by set theory

ArkType reduces every Type to a normalized set of constraints, so it knows which overlap, which contain others and which can't both be satisfied. Precompiling applies that in your build:

- **Unions discriminate themselves.** ArkType finds the key that tells a union's branches apart and switches on it, so data is checked against one branch rather than each in turn.
- **Redundant checks disappear.** `number > 0` intersected with `number >= 10` is `number >= 10`, one check, and a branch never rechecks the key it was chosen by.
- **Contradictions never ship.** `{ id: string }` intersected with `{ id: number }` throws a ParseError, which fails the build rather than shipping a validator that rejects everything.

### What ships

Edit the definition, and the precompiler runs on what you type:

```ts
const Shape = type({
	kind: "'circle'",
	radius: "number > 0"
}).or({
	kind: "'square'",
	side: "number > 0"
})
```

What ships for it, as the precompiler emits it:

```js
const check1 = function (data, ctx) {
	switch(data?.kind) {
		case "circle": return check2(data)
		case "square": return check3(data)
	}
	return false
}

const check2 = function (data, ctx) {
	for (;;) {
		if (!((check4(data.radius)))) {
			break
		}
		return true
	}
	return false
}

const check3 = function (data, ctx) {
	for (;;) {
		if (!((check4(data.side)))) {
			break
		}
		return true
	}
	return false
}

const check4 = function (data, ctx) {
	return (Number.isFinite(data)) && (data > 0)
}
```

## With agents

The build is quiet when everything precompiles, helpers included: ``const text = (max: number) => type(`0 < string <= ${max}`)`` precompiles at each call passing it values the build can read, like `text(50)`. Where it can't precompile a definition and the fix is clear, the build fails with the file, line and column, what it couldn't do, why, and how to fix it:

```
src/forms.ts:8:16  text(limit) cannot be precompiled
  `limit` is a parameter of makeField (src/forms.ts:7:27); its value is known only at runtime
  Write the definition where makeField is called, with the value it passes for `limit`, so the build precompiles each call.
```

To shorten the build-fix loop:

- Run [`arktype-precompile --check`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#check-an-existing-project) to list every definition the build would refuse, without bundling.
- Add the [ESLint rule](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#eslint) so the same errors show in the editor and in lint runs.
- Run tests in [shadow mode](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#shadow-mode), which fails a test wherever a precompiled validator would behave otherwise than arktype.
- Give your agent the [ArkType skill](https://arktype.io/docs/agents) so it writes definitions the build accepts on the first try.

## Build time

Precompiling moves creating your Types from your program's startup to your build, so a build takes longer. We timed an app of 1012 Types: 22 copies of our startup benchmark's SaaS schemas, each Type validating a request in a handler. Each figure is a median, with the plugin rather than without it, on Node 25 with 16 cores.

- A cold production build took 7.3 s rather than 414 ms with Vite 8, 8.2 s rather than 138 ms with esbuild and 20.3 s rather than 5.6 s with Next 16 on Turbopack.
- Vite's dev server loaded the app in a browser in 7.1 s rather than 1.1 s, and the page showed an edit to the module every Type in its copy imports in 2.6 s rather than 374 ms. Next's took 15.2 s rather than 4.1 s to load and 488 ms rather than 37 ms to show the edit.
- esbuild's watch rebuild after that edit took 1.7 s rather than 57 ms, and 5.7 s rather than 60 ms for a production bundle, which reads the whole app again to leave out what no read needs.

At 92 Types, the plugin added 1.0 s to Vite's production build, 1.3 s to esbuild's and 2.5 s to Next's, and 256 ms to an edit in Vite's dev server.

[Benchmarks](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/benchmarks) has how every number here was measured.

## How a validator differs

A standalone validator validates, asserts and implements Standard Schema as the Type it replaces does, with the same error messages. It doesn't compose or introspect: it lacks methods like `.and` and `.extends`. The build fails wherever it sees your program rely on what a validator lacks. See [Validators](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/validators).

If you need the whole Type API at runtime, build with `runtime: "arktype"`: arktype ships, and each Type the build could precompile skips compiling at runtime. [Dynamic vs Precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/dynamic-vs-precompiled) compares the three side by side.

# Dynamic vs Precompiled

> The same definitions, run two ways.

Every ArkType definition can run dynamically, created by `type()` at runtime, or [precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile), constructed when you build. It infers the same type either way, so you can switch at any time.

In our runs of schemabenchmarks.dev's product schema, dynamic ArkType validates valid data as fast as precompiled ArkType. What precompiling removes is everything around a Type's checks: the parser, the time it takes to create each Type, and the code it generates.

| | Dynamic | Precompiled | Precompiled with `runtime: "arktype"` |
| - | - | - | - |
| Build step | none | a bundler plugin or driver | a bundler plugin or driver |
| Ships arktype's parser | yes | no, only `arktype/runtime` | yes |
| Generates code at runtime | yes, unless [`jitless`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#jitless) | never | only for Types the build couldn't precompile |
| Composing at runtime | the whole Type API | inside definitions, which the build evaluates | the whole Type API |
| Introspection members | all | those the build sees read, or [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) sets | all |
| Error messages | arktype's | the same text, on issues [without `actual` or `propString`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/validators#errors) | arktype's |
| [Locales](https://arktype.io/docs/i18n) | yes | no | yes |
| Equal definitions | one Type | one validator, [but for a few cases](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#equal-definitions) | one Type |

## Equal definitions

arktype returns one Type for a scope's equal definitions written alike, and for spellings it normalizes alike, so `type("string[]") === type("string").array()`, in one module or across two. A precompiled program compares the same, including any function a Type holds, [but for a few cases](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#equal-definitions).

## Which to use

Precompile an app you bundle. Its validators ship without a parser or a JIT, and the build reports anything it can't precompile with the fix. See [Setup](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup), [Speed and size](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile#speed-and-size) for the numbers, and [Size at scale](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/size-at-scale) for what each mode costs as an app's Types grow.

Stay dynamic where there's no build, like a script or a REPL, or where definitions are only known at runtime. A standalone build can also leave those to arktype as [runtime islands](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands).

Build with `runtime: "arktype"` while you migrate, or where a program composes or introspects Types at runtime but still benefits from skipping the compile step.

# Setup

> Add precompilation to your bundler, framework, test runner or Node program.

## Installation

```bash
npm install -D @ark/aot
```

`@ark/aot` runs on Node 22.12 or later, and precompiles with the version of `arktype` it imports, so install one copy of `arktype`. The build fails if your program resolves another version, or more than one copy of `arktype`, naming each and the file that reached it. Each module of validators also imports an export of `arktype/runtime` named for its version, so a bundle or Node [fails to link](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/troubleshooting#setup) it to another version's runtime, like one a stale cache kept. That import adds nothing to the bundle.

`@ark/aot` peers on the exact `arktype` it was released with, so upgrade the two together. Renovate and Dependabot open a pull request for each unless you group them:

```json
{
	"packageRules": [
		{
			"matchPackageNames": ["arktype", "@ark/*"],
			"groupName": "arktype"
		}
	]
}
```

```yaml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: npm
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
    groups:
      arktype:
        patterns: ["arktype", "@ark/*"]
```

## Bundlers

`@ark/aot/unplugin` precompiles a program as your bundler builds it.

**Vite**

```ts
import { precompile } from "@ark/aot/unplugin"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({
	plugins: [precompile.vite()]
})
```

Vitest runs tests through the same plugin. With a framework, list it right after the framework's plugin, as [Frameworks](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#frameworks) shows.

On a server, Vite leaves a dependency external unless `ssr.noExternal` names it, and the plugin names only arktype's own packages and those you precompile. A dependency that imports arktype, like `@hono/arktype-validator`, would load it from Node, beside the runtime your validators use, and `out instanceof type.errors` would be false there, so a build fails naming what bundles it: `ssr.noExternal`, or [`dependencies`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#dependencies) for one that defines Types. One that only reads a Type it's passed, like hono-openapi, needs nothing set.

Only a build checks this, and only for a dependency that declares arktype in its `package.json`. `vite dev` and Vitest bundle nothing, so they load such a dependency from Node without failing, and `instanceof type.errors` stays false in it until you add it.

**esbuild**

```ts
import { precompile } from "@ark/aot/unplugin"
import { build } from "esbuild"

await build({
	entryPoints: ["src/main.ts"],
	// required, as precompiled modules import validators the bundle includes
	bundle: true,
	outfile: "dist/main.js",
	plugins: [precompile.esbuild()]
})
```

Put `precompile.esbuild()` ahead of any plugin that loads your TypeScript modules, since esbuild loads a module with the first plugin that returns it.

tsup takes it in `esbuildPlugins`, and leaves your dependencies external unless told to bundle them, so add `noExternal: ["arktype"]`. The build fails without it, as the program would load arktype beside the runtime its validators use.

**Rolldown**

```ts
import { precompile } from "@ark/aot/unplugin"
import { defineConfig } from "rolldown"

export default defineConfig({
	input: "src/main.ts",
	output: { file: "dist/main.js" },
	plugins: [precompile.rolldown()]
})
```

tsdown takes it in `plugins`, and leaves your dependencies external unless told to bundle them, so add `deps: { alwaysBundle: [/^arktype(\/|$)/] }`. The build fails without it, as the program would load arktype beside the runtime its validators use.

**Rollup**

```js
import { precompile } from "@ark/aot/unplugin"
import { nodeResolve } from "@rollup/plugin-node-resolve"
import typescript from "@rollup/plugin-typescript"

export default {
	input: "src/main.ts",
	output: { file: "dist/main.js", format: "es" },
	plugins: [
		precompile.rollup(),
		nodeResolve({ extensions: [".ts", ".js"] }),
		typescript()
	]
}
```

**webpack**

```js
import { precompile } from "@ark/aot/unplugin"

export default {
	entry: "./src/main.ts",
	resolve: { extensions: [".ts", ".js"] },
	module: {
		rules: [
			{ test: /\.ts$/, loader: "ts-loader", options: { transpileOnly: true } }
		]
	},
	plugins: [precompile.webpack()]
}
```

ts-loader is handed modules the plugin already precompiled, which import validators TypeScript can't see, so it only transpiles them. Check types with `tsc --noEmit`, or `fork-ts-checker-webpack-plugin`, which reads your sources.

A production build reads each module again as the loaders after the plugin built it, to fail where one adds a read of a validator, so they must emit ES modules: where your tsconfig sets `module` to `"commonjs"`, a pruned build fails, naming the loader, as it can't follow what CommonJS reads. Set `module` to `"esnext"`, or `prune: false`. A module that was CommonJS as it reached the plugin, like a workspace package tsc built, passes as it is, since the build keeps each member of what such a module loads with `require()`.

**Rspack**

```js
import { precompile } from "@ark/aot/unplugin"

export default {
	entry: "./src/main.ts",
	resolve: { extensions: [".ts", ".js"] },
	module: {
		rules: [
			{
				test: /\.ts$/,
				loader: "builtin:swc-loader",
				options: { jsc: { parser: { syntax: "typescript" } } },
				type: "javascript/auto"
			}
		]
	},
	plugins: [precompile.rspack()]
}
```

**Rsbuild**

```ts
import { precompile } from "@ark/aot/unplugin"
import { defineConfig } from "@rsbuild/core"

export default defineConfig({
	plugins: [precompile.rsbuild()]
})
```

**Bun**

```ts
import { precompile } from "@ark/aot/unplugin"

await Bun.build({
	entrypoints: ["src/main.ts"],
	outdir: "dist",
	target: "bun",
	plugins: [precompile.bun()]
})
```

`target: "bun"` builds a program Bun runs. Leave it out to bundle for a browser. Bun's bundler needs Bun 1.2.22 or later. To precompile as Bun runs your code, see [Bun](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#bun).

Bun handles what `external` names without asking the plugin, so the build fails for arktype's own packages there but can't check another that imports arktype. Leave one out of `external`, or it loads arktype beside the runtime your validators use, and `out instanceof type.errors` is false there.

**Others**

Farm takes `precompile.farm()` among its `plugins`:

```ts
import { precompile } from "@ark/aot/unplugin"
import { defineConfig } from "@farmfe/core"

export default defineConfig({
	plugins: [precompile.farm()]
})
```

For Next.js, see [Next.js](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#next).

By default, each definition becomes a standalone validator and `arktype` resolves to `arktype/runtime`. A dependency that imports `arktype` gets `arktype/runtime` too, where defining a Type throws, so the build fails for each such package unless it [opts in](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#libraries).

## Options in ark.json

Set [options](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options) in `ark.json` beside your `package.json` rather than in the plugin call, so `arktype-precompile --check`, the Node and Bun drivers and the ESLint rule build as your bundler does. A program that calls `configure()` names its config module there:

```json
{
	"$schema": "./node_modules/@ark/aot/ark.schema.json",
	"precompile": {
		"config": "./src/arktype.config.ts"
	}
}
```

The same settings can go under an `"ark"` key in `package.json` instead; see [ark.json](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#arkjson).

A validator ships its JSON Schema where the build sees code read it, so a library that converts it, like the MCP SDK, the AI SDK or hono-openapi, needs nothing set. [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) describes how the build decides, and only overrides it.

## Cache

A build keeps each module it precompiles in `node_modules/.cache/ark`, in the directory it runs from, so a later build, dev server or Next.js process can reuse it. An entry is read only while everything its build had read when it wrote the entry is the same: the code of `@ark/aot` and `arktype`, a linked or repacked copy included, the version of Node, the module's source, each file the precompiler had read, what each import had resolved to, and your settings. That includes files the module doesn't import, so the cache serves a build where nothing changed, while a build after you edit a module reuses only what was written before that module was first read, which can be little. A pruned production build or `arktype-precompile --emit` reads the whole program, so it reuses nothing once any module changes. A watch build or dev server stores only what it precompiles before its first change, keeping what it precompiles again to itself. A webpack or Rspack persistent cache is versioned by the same code and your settings, so it rebuilds each module once either changes. Deleting the directory is always safe, as the next build writes it again. An entry is code your bundle runs, checked only for a write cut short, so restore the directory from a CI cache only where nothing less trusted than the build, like a pull request from a fork, can write that cache, as for Vite's or webpack's.

## Frameworks

With Vite, list `precompile.vite()` right after your framework's plugin, and ahead of `react()`, a Babel plugin like the React Compiler's or another that rewrites modules, so the build reads your modules as you wrote them. Each line was checked with a production build of a small app, on SvelteKit 3.1, Astro 7.4, Nuxt 4.6, React Router 8.5, TanStack Router 1.168, Cloudflare's Vite plugin 1.65 with Wrangler 4.153, and Metro 0.87:

| Framework | Setup |
| - | - |
| SvelteKit | `plugins: [sveltekit(), precompile.vite()]` in `vite.config.ts` |
| Astro | `vite: { plugins: [precompile.vite()] }` in `astro.config.ts` |
| Nuxt | `vite: { plugins: [precompile.vite()] }` and `nitro: { rollupConfig: { plugins: [precompile.rollup({ prune: process.env.NODE_ENV === "production" })] } }` in `nuxt.config.ts`. Nitro bundles server routes and `shared/` itself, with Rollup, so without the second it ships arktype whole, and as Rollup has no production mode, `prune` has `nuxt build` [prune](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#prune) them but not `nuxt dev` |
| React Router (Remix) | `plugins: [reactRouter(), precompile.vite()]` in `vite.config.ts` |
| TanStack Router | `plugins: [tanstackRouter({ target: "react", autoCodeSplitting: true }), precompile.vite(), react()]` in `vite.config.ts`. Its code splitting moves a route's component into a module of its own after the plugins ahead of it run, so the build fails where arktype's plugin comes first |
| Next.js | See [Next.js](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#next) |
| Cloudflare Workers | With `@cloudflare/vite-plugin`, `plugins: [cloudflare(), precompile.vite()]` in `vite.config.ts`. Wrangler bundles with esbuild but takes no plugins, so without Vite, build the worker with esbuild and `precompile.esbuild()` from Wrangler's `build.command`, and point `main` at its output. Workers don't let arktype compile a validator as it runs, which a precompiled one doesn't need |
| Monorepos | Nothing extra. A workspace package linked into `node_modules`, as pnpm, npm, Yarn and Bun workspaces link it, resolves to its own directory, so the build precompiles it with the program. It reads what the package's `exports` point at: its TypeScript source, ES modules, or the CommonJS tsc built it to, whose `exports.a = ...`, `export *` and `export * as` it reads as tsc writes them. See [Next.js with webpack in a monorepo](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#next-monorepo) for an app |
| Jest | Not supported. See [Test runners](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#test-runners) |
| Deno | A bundler plugin works under Deno, e.g. `deno run -A npm:vite build` with `precompile.vite()`. There's no driver, so `deno run` on your source loads arktype unprecompiled |
| React Native (Metro) | Not supported as a plugin. See [React Native (Metro)](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#metro) to precompile the package defining your Types, which the app imports |
| Parcel | Not supported. Bundle with a [supported bundler](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#bundlers) |

Define your Types in `.ts` or `.js` modules. A component another plugin compiles, like a Svelte, Vue or Astro component or an MDX page, can call a validator or read its `.allows` and `.assert`, but the build can't write a validator inside it. So a read there that only a precompiled site could serve, like `.description` or `.omit()`, or that a validator lacks, like `.errors`, fails the build, or the dev server's request for the component, naming the read. Move it into a module the component imports, e.g. as a function the component calls.

A production build reads each component as its framework compiles it, and each virtual module, like SvelteKit's `$env/static/private`, so it [prunes](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#prune) through them. Where something still keeps it from pruning, like `import.meta.glob()` or a validator passed to a form library's adapter, it warns once, saying why.

## Next.js

With Turbopack, the default, export your config through `withPrecompile`, add the loader as a rule for each extension your definitions and config module are in, and for JavaScript that mentions arktype, which checks your dependencies, then alias arktype's entries to the runtime, and `arktype/schema/runtime` to the one the loader writes for your options:

```js
import { withPrecompile } from "@ark/aot/turbopack"

export default withPrecompile({
	// for the pages router
	bundlePagesRouterDependencies: true,
	turbopack: {
		rules: {
			"*.ts": { loaders: ["@ark/aot/turbopack"] },
			"*.tsx": { loaders: ["@ark/aot/turbopack"] },
			"*.{js,mjs}": {
				condition: { content: /arktype/ },
				loaders: ["@ark/aot/turbopack"]
			}
		},
		resolveAlias: {
			arktype: "arktype/runtime",
			"arktype/codecs": "arktype/runtime",
			"arktype/config": "arktype/runtime",
			"arktype/errors": "arktype/runtime",
			"arktype/mutatesInput": "arktype/runtime",
			"arktype/schema/runtime": "@ark/aot/turbopack/runtime"
		}
	}
})
```

`withPrecompile` also takes a function, as Next does. The loader fails a module whose `arktype` imports resolve otherwise, naming the aliases to add. With `runtime: "arktype"` or `shadow: true`, leave the `arktype` aliases out, since the loader fails a module they resolve to the runtime. `@ark/aot/turbopack/runtime` re-exports the copy of `arktype/schema/runtime` your options load, like the one [`errors: "none"`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#errors) does, so the aliases stay alike as you change them. It reruns when a module's local imports change, and applies a changed configuration once the dev server restarts.

The aliases also point a dependency's `arktype` imports at the runtime, so the `*.{js,mjs}` rule has the loader fail the build for a dependency that defines Types but doesn't [opt in](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#libraries), and precompile one that does or that [`dependencies`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#dependencies) sets to `"aot"`. Turbopack can't run one dependency on arktype, so for one that creates Types from values it reads as it runs, like `drizzle-arktype`, build with webpack or with `runtime: "arktype"`. The loader reads only `import` and `export` declarations, so a CommonJS dependency that `require`s arktype throws `type is not a function` when it loads instead.

On the pages router's server, Next otherwise leaves dependencies external, where the aliases don't reach, so Node would load arktype, for your code and for any dependency importing it, beside the runtime your validators use, and `out instanceof type.errors` would be false for their errors. `bundlePagesRouterDependencies` has Next bundle them, as it does the app router's, and the loader fails a module there without it. `transpilePackages: ["arktype"]` isn't enough, as a dependency left external still loads its own copy. Either router leaves external a package `serverExternalPackages` names, so the loader fails the build for one that imports arktype, reading the list from `next.config` without running it: name its packages as string literals.

`withPrecompile` has `next build` read your project as Next loads `next.config`, before Turbopack starts, through every script under it that nothing imports and each route, so it can [prune](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#prune) and hold each validator once, in a file under `node_modules/.bin/.ark`. As the read writes only what changed, before Turbopack looks, Turbopack's build cache keeps from an earlier build only what this one's read left as it was. The read resolves imports as Node does, through your `tsconfig.json`'s `paths` and `turbopack.resolveAlias`, and the loader checks each module as Turbopack builds it against what it read, for each layer of a route, failing one that differs, naming it: a module a loader rewrote, or one whose import resolves to another file in that layer, as a `react-server` condition may. Where it can't read the project, it warns, naming why, and each module holds its own validators, as they do with `prune: false`, in `next dev` and without `withPrecompile`: for another loader in `turbopack.rules`, a Babel config like `.babelrc` or `experimental.swcPlugins`, which Turbopack runs after the loader, `pageExtensions`, a file like `.mdx` that a loader compiles, a query on an import, or an import it can't name.

Turbopack runs the loader in a pool of processes, once for the client and once for the server. `next dev` precompiles each module for each, where one process of `next build` precompiles its project once.

With webpack, which Next 15 builds with, as does `next build --webpack`, add the plugin, which fails the build where Next would leave arktype, or a package importing it, external:

```js
import { precompile } from "@ark/aot/unplugin"

export default {
	// for the pages router
	bundlePagesRouterDependencies: true,
	webpack: config => {
		config.plugins.push(precompile.webpack())
		return config
	}
}
```

`next dev` precompiles each module as a request first needs it, with either bundler, and rebuilds the modules that import a Type as you edit it, including one in a workspace package that `transpilePackages` names. A definition that throws fails the request with its error, and the next save that fixes it recovers. A change to `ark.json` fails each module built after it, naming the file, until you restart the server, and a restart builds under the new settings, not the earlier server's cache.

### Next.js with webpack in a monorepo

For an app in a workspace, on the pages router, whose `next.config.js` is CommonJS, this is the whole setup. Node 22.12 or later loads the plugin with `require`:

```js
const { precompile } = require("@ark/aot/unplugin")

module.exports = {
	// bundles arktype on the pages router's server, leaving its other
	// dependencies external, as bundlePagesRouterDependencies wouldn't
	transpilePackages: ["arktype", "arkregex"],
	webpack: config => {
		config.plugins.push(precompile.webpack())
		return config
	}
}
```

Add the two to a `transpilePackages` you already set, and the plugin to a `webpack` function you already have, before it returns. The plugin reads each module Next leaves external, and fails the build, naming the package to add, where one still loads arktype. `bundlePagesRouterDependencies: true` bundles every dependency instead, and is what Turbopack needs.

Check the app before its first build, from its directory, which takes seconds where the build takes minutes:

```sh
npx @ark/aot --check
```

Nothing else is set for the workspace:

- A workspace package is precompiled with the app, whether its `exports` point at TypeScript source or at what tsc built. The build reads a CommonJS module as tsc writes it, so a definition can read a const object a built package exports, like `type.enumerated(...Object.values(Plan.Enum))`, or call a helper it exports. [Troubleshooting](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/troubleshooting#reads) covers the exports it can't read.
- An alias in `tsconfig.json`'s `paths`, like `@app/*`, resolves for every file under that tsconfig, including a test its `include` leaves out.
- `experimental.optimizePackageImports` stays as it is. Next.js builds the entry of each package it lists once for each set of names imported from it, and the build reads each of those modules as the entry's file, so it still reads the bundle whole and [prunes](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#prune).
- A definition can read an object that a package built to CommonJS shares between its modules, like an enum. `require()` hands each of them the whole module, so the build can't tell that none writes it, and the validator checks the value it read as it's created, as it does in every build.
- An `import()` of a computed specifier, like ``import(`./icons/${name}`)``, doesn't keep the build from pruning: webpack builds a module for each file the specifier can name, and the build keeps each member only where one of them exports a validator.

Leave [`prune`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#prune) unset. A build that can't read the bundle whole warns `prune: off, because ...`, naming what kept it from reading it, and builds every validator whole, which can cost more than arktype did. Where the build warns that it bakes each introspection member, set the [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) no code reads to `false`, as the warning lists them. An app holding many Types that validates input as it arrives, like forms, is smallest built with [`preset: "smallest"`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#choosing-smallest).

## Node

### Run a program

The Node driver, on Node 22.15 or later, precompiles each module as it loads, for `node --test` or any program:

```ts
import { register } from "@ark/aot/node"

register()
```

```sh
node --import ./register.ts src/main.ts
node --import ./register.ts --test
```

Pass `--enable-source-maps` for original lines in stack traces.

### Build with tsc

A program `tsc` compiles to run from its `outDir` precompiles what it emits with `--emit`, run after `tsc`:

```json
{
	"scripts": {
		"build": "tsc && arktype-precompile --emit"
	}
}
```

It reads the nearest `tsconfig.json`, or the one `--tsconfig` names, and the tsconfigs it references. Each module reading arktype, directly or through a Type it imports, is precompiled from its source as a bundler would and emitted again over what `tsc` wrote, in the module format, target and source maps the tsconfig sets, with `arktype` and its other entries imported or required as `arktype/runtime`. Other modules and declarations stay as `tsc` emitted them. It takes the options `--check` does, reads `ark.json`, and fails on what a build would, writing nothing. Since it emits from source, run anything that rewrites `tsc`'s output, like `tsc-alias`, after it.

Dependencies are left to Node, so one that imports `arktype` loads it beside the runtime rather than failing the build. That includes one that [opts in](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#libraries), whose Types are arktype's at runtime, so a definition reading one of them fails the build, naming the fix. `errors: "none"` and `optimizeErrors: "size"`, which `preset: "smallest"` sets, need a copy of `arktype/schema/runtime` that only a bundler or the Node driver can load in place of the one `arktype/runtime` imports, so `--emit` refuses them. A library publishes what `tsc` emits without `--emit`, and [opts in](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#libraries) so its consumers' builds precompile it.

`--emit --declare` also writes [declarations](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#declarations) as `--declare` does. `--emit` reads the compiler API of TypeScript 5.5 to 6, so in a TypeScript 7 project, install TypeScript 6 beside it: `npm i -D typescript-6@npm:typescript@6` (which `--declare` also reads before TypeScript 7.1).

## Bun

To precompile as Bun loads your code, for `bun test` or any program, register the plugin from a file `bunfig.toml` preloads. `bun test` reads only the `preload` in its `[test]` section, so list the file in both:

```ts
import { precompile } from "@ark/aot/bun"

Bun.plugin(precompile())
```

```toml
preload = ["./preload.ts"]

[test]
preload = ["./preload.ts"]
```

Bun doesn't ask a runtime plugin to resolve packages, so `arktype` resolves to the runtime `cwd` resolves for every importer, and dependencies aren't checked for copies of arktype. To bundle with Bun, use `precompile.bun()` from [`@ark/aot/unplugin`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#bundlers).

## React Native (Metro)

Metro has no plugin: it caches each module by its own text, so a module whose validators are written from a Type it imports would keep them after that Type changed. Precompile the package that defines your Types instead, with `tsc` and [`--emit`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#tsc), and have the app import what it emits. Metro bundles that as it does any package, and the bundle holds each validator and `arktype`'s runtime, without its parser:

```json
{
	"name": "@app/domain",
	"type": "module",
	"sideEffects": false,
	"exports": {
		".": { "types": "./out/index.d.ts", "default": "./out/index.js" }
	},
	"scripts": {
		"build": "tsc && arktype-precompile --emit --declare"
	},
	"peerDependencies": { "arktype": "*" }
}
```

```json
{
	"compilerOptions": {
		"target": "ES2022",
		"module": "ESNext",
		"moduleResolution": "Bundler",
		"rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true,
		"allowImportingTsExtensions": true,
		"rootDir": "src",
		"outDir": "out"
	},
	"include": ["src"]
}
```

- Leave `declaration` unset and let `--declare` write the declarations. `tsc` can't write one for a [cyclic](https://arktype.io/docs/scopes#cyclic-types) scope, and fails with `TS5088`, where `--declare` names each cycle. Under TypeScript 7, install `typescript-6@npm:typescript@6` beside it [as above](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#tsc).
- Import the package's own modules with their `.ts` extensions, which `rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` writes as `.js` in `out`. Metro reads those imports from either, but it doesn't resolve a `.js` import to the `.ts` file beside it.
- Each emitted module imports `arktype/runtime`, which Metro resolves through arktype's `exports`. That's on by default in Metro 0.87, and set by `resolver.unstable_enablePackageExports` in earlier versions. Install `arktype` where the package resolves it, as a dependency of the package, and let a monorepo's `watchFolders` include the package and `arktype`.
- Rebuild the package as you edit a Type. A Metro dev server bundles the next request from the new `out`, since each emitted module holds the validators of the Types it imports in its own text.
- A Type another module of the package composes has only the introspection members that module reads of it, so `description` or `toJsonSchema` read `undefined` in the app unless something bakes them. Set [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) in the package's `ark.json` for each one the app reads.

Have the package re-export `type` and `ArkErrors`, so the app checks an error against the runtime its validators use:

```ts
export * from "./money.ts"
export { type, ArkErrors } from "arktype"
```

An app that imports `arktype` itself bundles its parser and a second copy of the runtime, where `out instanceof type.errors` is false for the package's errors. A validator the package exports lacks the members a Type has beyond validating, like `.and()` and `.array()`, so write each Type you compose in the package, where a definition may name another Type.

Checked with Metro 0.87 and `@react-native/babel-preset` for iOS and Android bundles, minified and in development, which matched the bundle Metro built from the package's source, and a bundle also ran in Hermes 0.13.

## Test runners

Each driver takes the plugin's options, fails on the same errors, except that Bun's doesn't check dependencies, and resolves `arktype` to `arktype/runtime` where its host allows. The precompiler runs in a worker thread, sharing no module state with your program.

- **Vitest** uses the Vite plugin from your `vite.config.ts` or `vitest.config.ts`.
- **`node --test`** uses the [Node driver](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#node).
- **`bun test`** uses the [Bun driver](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#bun).
- **Jest** has no driver, so it runs your Types with arktype, unprecompiled. Your definitions behave the same either way, but to test the validators you ship, run tests with one of the above.

A test file is an entry of its own, so in a program with a [config module](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#configuration), the first validator a test file loads throws that it was created before `configure()` ran, unless the config module loads first. List it in Vitest's `test.setupFiles`, after the plugin in the `[test]` preload of `bunfig.toml`, or after the Node driver: `node --import ./register.ts --import ./src/arktype.config.ts --test`.

To test that your precompiled validators behave as arktype does, run tests in [shadow mode](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#shadow-mode).

## Not supported

Some tools and modules can't be precompiled. [Troubleshooting](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/troubleshooting#not-supported) lists each, with the error the build reports and what to do instead.

## Check an existing project

`--check` lists the definitions that can't be precompiled, and why, without bundling (also runnable via `pnpm exec arktype-precompile --check` or `arktype`'s `ark check` — use `npx arktype check` outside an installed project, since `ark` on npm is an unrelated package):

```sh
npx @ark/aot --check src
```

```
src/forms.ts:5:21  accepted
src/forms.ts:14:19  type(`string <= ${limit}`) cannot be precompiled
  `limit` is a parameter of makeField (src/forms.ts:12:22); its value is known only at runtime
  Write the definition where makeField is called, with the value it passes for `limit`, so the build precompiles each call.
```

A directory, like `src`, stands for each JavaScript and TypeScript file it holds. Without a pattern, it checks every JavaScript and TypeScript file under the current directory outside `node_modules`, `dist`, `out` and `build`. It also checks each script outside the current directory that one it checks imports, as the build transforms it too, like a workspace package's source. Where `NODE_ENV` is `production`, it also prints the warning a production bundle of those files would give where it [can't prune](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#prune). It reads no Svelte, Vue or Astro component or MDX page, whose reads of a validator only its framework's compiled code shows, so it names those under the current directory that import a module, which only the build checks.

It reads [`ark.json`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#arkjson) as a build does, and the options a plugin call passes in a file at the project's root, like `precompile.vite({ config: "src/config.ts" })` in `vite.config.ts`, saying where it found them. An option that isn't a literal there, or a plugin loaded in a way it can't follow, fails it, asking for the option in `ark.json` or as a flag. Each [option](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options) is a flag that overrides both, like `--preset smallest`, `--optimize-errors size`, `--no-freeze` or `--members '{"assert":false}'`.

It exits with 1 where the build would fail. `--fail-under <percent>` exits with 1 only if less than that percent of definitions can be precompiled, or on an error outside a definition, so CI can hold a project to it while it migrates.

The same analysis is available as `new Precompiler(host, options).analyze(source, id)` from `@ark/aot`, which, as a build does, applies the program's configuration to arktype in its thread.

## ESLint

The ESLint rules report what the build would, as you edit:

```js
import { configs } from "@ark/aot/eslint"
import tseslint from "typescript-eslint"

export default [
	{
		files: ["**/*.{ts,mts,cts,tsx}"],
		languageOptions: { parser: tseslint.parser }
	},
	configs.recommended
]
```

`configs.recommended` lints JavaScript and TypeScript files. It reports what fails the build as an error, through `@ark/aot/precompilable`, and what the build warns about, like a problem [`allowUnsafe`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#allowunsafe) builds past, as a warning, through `@ark/aot/warnings`. Each takes the build's options, which `ark.json` gives both. ESLint parses TypeScript only through a parser like typescript-eslint's, which a project already linting TypeScript configures.

# Validators

> What a precompiled Type is, and how it differs from one arktype creates.

## Standalone validators

In a standalone build, each Type your program defines becomes a validator running on `arktype/runtime`. Call it, `.assert()` with it or pass it as a [Standard Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/standard-schema), as you would the Type:

```ts
// bundled as a validator
export const User = type({ name: "string > 0" })

const out = User(data)

if (out instanceof type.errors) console.error(out.summary)
```

Scopes, Modules, Generics, cyclic Types, `match`, `type.fn` and [codecs](https://arktype.io/docs/codecs) are precompiled too. A Module becomes a plain object of its validators, and a Scope or Generic an empty object, since resolving an alias or instantiating a Generic needs arktype. A call to `define`, which returns its argument, is replaced by the argument.

A definition holding functions, like a narrow, a morph or a class, becomes a call to a factory passing each one where the definition was written. The factory checks at creation that each class, and each function another module supplies, is what its code was compiled for, and throws if not.

In a [production bundle](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#prune), a narrow written in its definition is written with the validator's code instead of being passed, where it reads only its parameters, what it declares, and what its module imports from modules that only declare functions and values their text fixes, like a file of helpers. The validator's code then imports such a module itself, which may load it before the module defining the Type would have, and loading it runs nothing. A narrow reading anything else, like a value its own module declares or an import of a module that runs a call as it loads, is passed as above.

## What a validator has

Besides being called, a validator has `allows()`, and by default `assert()`, `meta`, `~standard`, `traverse()`, `from()` and `toString()`. `expression`, `description`, `json`, `toJSON()`, `toJsonSchema()` and `~standard.jsonSchema` are baked as arktype returns them, each into the validators the build sees code read it off, its dependencies' included, so the MCP SDK, the AI SDK, Elysia's OpenAPI plugin, hono-openapi and oRPC's converter get a JSON Schema with nothing to set. The [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) option bakes one into every validator or none instead, and says how the build decides. A read the build sees in the program, like `User.expression`, is replaced by its value either way. Reading one a validator lacks reads `undefined`, and where `arktype/runtime` resolves under the [`"development"` condition](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/validators#errors), also warns, naming the member and the setting.

It lacks the methods that compose or relate a Type, like `.and`, `.or`, `.in` or `.extends`. The build fails where it sees one read outside a definition it precompiles, including off a value it lost track of after a Type reached it, and, once for each import, off an import it can't resolve:

```
main.ts:8:29  Long.description reads description, which a standalone validator lacks
  `Long` is a Type, which the standalone runtime replaces with a validator, and no precompiled site covers the read
  Standalone builds do not ship arktype. Use it inside a precompiled definition, or build with runtime: "arktype".
```

The build resolves an import as TypeScript does, and where that fails, a bundler's plugin or loader asks the bundler, so an import only an alias in the bundler's config names, like Nuxt's `#shared` without its `tsconfig.json`, is checked like any other. `--check`, the ESLint rule, Bun and the Node driver resolve as TypeScript does alone. An alias in `tsconfig.json`'s `paths` resolves for every file under that tsconfig, including one its `include` leaves out, like a test beside `src`. A module the import resolves to is read as an ES module, or as the CommonJS tsc writes: `exports.a = ...`, `export *` and `export * as`.

The members that exist only as types, `infer`, `inferIn`, `inferOut`, `inferIntrospectableOut` and `t`, are `undefined` on a Type too, so reading one is never reported, as in `typeof User.infer.address`.

Composing inside a definition is fine, since the build evaluates it: `export const Admin = User.and({ role: "'admin'" })` is precompiled to a validator of its own, as is composing the Type a call to a helper returns, like `addressOf(saved).or("undefined")`. Where the build refused the definition of `User` itself, the read is reported as ``User.and composes `User`, which can't be precompiled``, under the reasons of that definition's own report. So is [`.encode`](https://arktype.io/docs/codecs#precompiling) wherever the build sees it read, like `const encode = (event: unknown) => Event.encode(event)`, where its module imports `arktype/codecs`.

A validator and its members are frozen, except a Date or RegExp it holds, unless the build sets [`freeze: false`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#freeze), as a [production build](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#production-builds) does by default.

## Errors

A validator returns errors of its own, instances of `type.errors` and of `arktype`'s `ArkErrors`. Each issue holds the failed check's `code`, `path`, `data` and `expected`, with a `message` like `must be a string`, which `summary` writes after its path, as `name must be a string`:

- Its messages, `expected`, `summary` and the message `assert` throws are the text arktype writes for the same failure, so tests and logs read alike in development and production. A [`message` you configure](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#message) is written after its path and a colon in both, like `email: Enter a valid email`, unless it [begins as arktype's own would](https://arktype.io/docs/errors#summary-lines). A union no branch allows is one issue whose `errors` hold each branch's first, written as arktype lists them, as in `a must be a string or b must be a string`. The first union in a bundle that lists what its branches expected ships about 0.5 kB gzipped to write it, and a bundle with none ships nothing for it.
- An issue has no `actual` or `propString`. Neither a validator's message nor arktype's writes what a value was unless `actual` is configured or passed to `ctx.reject`, but a missing key's message says `(was missing)` in both. A `message` writer you configure reads `actual`, the data's description, as in arktype.
- An issue a `pipe.try` morph raises by throwing says what was thrown, as arktype's does, but has no `morph` or `cause`.
- An issue a narrow or morph raises is written from the `code`, `path`, `relativePath`, `prefixPath`, `data`, `expected`, `description`, `actual` and `message` it passes `ctx.reject()` or `ctx.error()`, while arktype's keeps every key it's passed. The build fails where one passes `meta`, or another key without a `code`, in an object literal, as in `ctx.reject({ flags: FLAG, message: "Must be unique." })`, since reading `issue.flags` would find it in development and not in production. A code's own context, like `rule` in `ctx.reject({ code: "minLength", rule: 2 })`, which its type requires, builds, though only its text is kept. Read what the program needs from what's kept, or make the definition a [runtime island](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands).
- A validator a morph calls with its `ctx` adds its issues to that validation.
- [`byPath`, `flatByPath`, `flatMessagesByPath` and `byAncestorPath`](https://arktype.io/docs/errors#arkerrors) read a validator's errors as they read arktype's, keying each path as arktype writes it, like `items[0].id`. `arktype/runtime` doesn't export `messageIn`, and calls to it fail the build; `summaryIn()` returns `summary`, while passing a locale fails the build and requires a [runtime island](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands).
- [`firstIssue(out)`](https://arktype.io/docs/errors#finding-only-the-first) finds only the first issue of errors that haven't found theirs, stopping where the data first fails.
- A `message`, `expected` or `actual` configured for a code or on a Type is written as arktype writes it. A build configured with what a validator can't write, like a locale, [fails with its fix](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#configuration).
- They aren't instances of `arktype/schema`'s `ArkErrors`, so the build fails where a module imports that one.
- `console.log` prints them by name, as `ArkErrors { summary, issues }`, where `arktype/runtime` resolves under the `"development"` condition: Vite's dev server, Vitest, webpack's development mode, and Node or esbuild given `--conditions=development`. There, reading an introspection member a validator's build didn't bake also warns, with the [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) setting that bakes it, and reads `undefined` as in production. A production build ships nothing for either.

The [`errors`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#errors) option ships less: one issue, or one saying the data is invalid.

## Shipping arktype instead

`runtime: "arktype"` ships arktype, leaving definitions as written: each stays a Type with its whole API, and the build registers the code arktype would compile for it, so it skips compiling at runtime. A definition the build can't precompile is compiled at runtime as usual. [Which to use](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/dynamic-vs-precompiled#which-to-use) says when to choose it.

```ts
precompile.vite({ runtime: "arktype" })
```

To leave only some definitions to arktype in a standalone build, mark them as [runtime islands](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands).

## Limits

- `require("arktype")` or `import("arktype")` fails the build, since it would load arktype/runtime where the build precompiles no definition, but one whose specifier isn't a string literal isn't seen.
- The build fails for a definition reading an object or array the program writes before it, but doesn't see a write by a module other than the object's and the definition's, or through a call it can't follow. If one changed the object, the definition throws as it's created, naming the object and what the build read.
- The build doesn't see a Type reach a value through `arguments`, a generator, `Reflect.get`, `import()` or a namespace read at a runtime key, nor a direct `eval` or `with` changing a binding a definition reads. A Type it never sees reach a value is missed: calling a member it lacks throws, and reading one reads `undefined`.
- The build fails where it sees a Type's keys listed, as by `Object.keys(User)`, `for...in` or a spread, since a validator's differ. Where it can't tell a Type reaches the value, as through `await`, `import()` or a `Proxy`, the keys listed are the validator's.
- A module importing neither arktype nor a module exporting a Type isn't checked, so a member one of its functions reads off a Type passed to it is missed. Annotating the parameter with arktype's `Type` has the build check it.
- Inside a function the build can't see every call to, like an exported function, a method or a callback, reading `expression`, `description`, `json`, `toJSON()` or `toJsonSchema()` off a parameter isn't checked, since it's usually some other object's. Passed a Type, such a read reads the member the build bakes where it follows the Type there, and where it doesn't, reads `undefined`, and warns in development. Annotate the parameter with arktype's `Type` so the build checks it, or mark the Type's definition as a [runtime island](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands). The same goes for a field an exported class's constructor sets from a parameter, read off an instance, and for a Vue template reading a Type that `setup()` or `data()` exposes from a `<script lang="ts">` block; script setup and a plain `<script>` are checked.
- A definition whose branches arktype orders by the names of the functions they hold, like `type.instanceOf(Cat).or(type.instanceOf(Dog))`, is reported, since a minifier can rename them.
- A definition holding a function a parameter holds, or resolving a Scope alias a thunk defines whose Type holds one, is reported. Mark it as a [runtime island](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands).
- A definition holding a Standard Schema that isn't a Type, like a Zod schema, is reported. Define the schema with ArkType, or mark the definition as a [runtime island](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands).
- A union whose branches print alike once their functions are named prints as `X or X` where arktype prints `X`.
- A Date or RegExp a Type holds is one object for every Type and validation holding it.
- A builtin class a Type holds, like `Uint8Array`, is read as the validator's module loads, so a later polyfill isn't seen.
- When a validator rejects an array, it may look for errors only from the first element it rejects, so a getter or `Proxy` trap reading an element before that one runs once rather than twice.
- A validator may read a key a different number of times than arktype does, so a getter or `Proxy` trap answering differently between reads can pass or fail differently. arktype's own first call and later calls differ the same way.
- The `ctx.config` a narrow or morph receives holds only `jitless` and `onFail`.
- A module of validators fails to link to an `arktype/runtime` of another version, but nothing checks at runtime that `arktype` loads only for runtime islands.

# Options

> Ship less, and configure a precompiled program.

A standalone build can leave out what your program doesn't need. Set options in [`ark.json`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#arkjson), or in a plugin, driver or CLI call:

```ts
precompile.vite({
	errors: "none",
	mutatesInput: "always",
	members: { assert: false }
})
```

`errors`, `mutatesInput`, `members`, `optimize`, `optimizeErrors`, `strategies`, `schemas`, `freeze`, `lazy`, `creationChecks`, `jsonInput`, `bakedLimit`, `shadow`, `prune` and `dependencies` take effect in standalone mode alone, so setting one with `runtime: "arktype"` fails the build.

## Presets

A preset sets options for one goal, and any option set elsewhere overrides it:

```ts
precompile.vite({ preset: "smallest", members: { meta: false } })
```

| Preset | Sets | Gives up |
| - | - | - |
| `"smallest"` | `optimize: "size"`, `lazy: false` | speed, runtime islands, creating validators as first read |
| `"introspectable"` | each introspection member in [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) | size |

No preset changes what a program observes: none sets `errors`, `mutatesInput` or `jsonInput`, or drops a member some code may read, since the build can't see a member read by code it doesn't build, like a library reading `~standard`. A [production bundle](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#prune) leaves out the members it proves nothing reads. With `runtime: "arktype"`, a preset sets nothing.

### Choosing smallest

The default build compiles each validator to the code that checks its Type fastest. `"smallest"` writes it as calls to a runtime of small checkers, shared by every validator, so each Type adds about what its definition says. The more Types a bundle holds, the more that saves:

| App, gzipped production bundle | Default | `"smallest"` | Valibot |
| - | - | - | - |
| a login form, 1 Type | 1.2 KB | 1.0 KB | 1.7 KB |
| a shop, 23 Types | 5.1 KB | 3.5 KB | 3.6 KB |
| 10 Types | 4.1 KB | 3.2 KB | 3.4 KB |
| 50 Types | 11.5 KB | 5.4 KB | 5.5 KB |
| 200 Types | 33.7 KB | 11.0 KB | 11.3 KB |
| 1,000 Types | 139 KB | 37.2 KB | 39.5 KB |

What it costs is speed: the shared checkers validate more slowly than code compiled for each Type, and with [`lazy: false`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#lazy) the bundle creates every validator as it loads, so it starts more slowly too. In our runs of moltar's benchmark, counting instructions per call, "smallest" is 4% slower than Valibot on parseSafe and 2.1-2.6x faster on the other three cases, while Zod 4 is 1.5-7.9x faster than it and the default build 13-46x faster. [How it was counted](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/blob/main/ark/repo/bench/external/README.md#the-smallest-presets-speed). The [benchmarks](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/benchmarks) measure the default build. Choose `"smallest"` where your bundle holds more than a handful of Types and validates input as it arrives, like a frontend's forms and API responses. Keep the default for a server and for validation on a hot path. A program with both chooses [for each definition](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#strategies-and-schemas). A program reading only [`.allows`](https://arktype.io/docs/type-api) gets each validator written as the function checking it, as the default writes it, so it's no larger built `"smallest"`.

Compiled code grows with each Type, and arktype doesn't, so a program with enough Types, or Types large enough, is larger compiled than it would be shipping arktype. A [production bundle](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#prune) built with `optimize` unset estimates that from the code it wrote. Where its validators would outweigh arktype and a browser loads the bundle, as esbuild's `platform`, a webpack or Rspack compiler's `target`, Bun's `target` or a Vite client build says, the build writes them as `optimize: "size"` does instead, reading the bundle a second time, and warns that it did. It keeps the errors `optimizeErrors: "speed"` writes unless you set that, and leaves `lazy` as it was, so `"smallest"` is smaller still. A server's bundle stays compiled, as nothing downloads it. A build that can't tell what loads its bundle only warns: Turbopack's, whose one read holds the server's modules with the browser's, a Vite build of several environments, and a Rollup or Rolldown build. Set `optimize: "size"` or `"smallest"` to build so without the warning or the second read, or `optimize: "speed"` to keep them compiled. [Size at scale](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/size-at-scale) measures each build, dynamic arktype and other libraries as an app's Types grow, with and without messages and narrows.

A [production bundle](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#prune) built as one chunk by `"smallest"` also decides, from the Types it holds, how to write them smallest: checkers or compiled code, each validator declared once among the checkers others read, what many validators repeat made once, and common Types like `1 <= string <= 50`, `number.integer >= 0`, `string[] <= 10` and `string | null` as checkers of their own where enough of them repay that runtime. A Type that can't be written as a checker, like one in a cycle or a morph reading its `ctx`, stays compiled, and a bundle ships what morphs, aliases and narrows reading their `ctx` need only if it holds one. A narrow that tests its data and otherwise only rejects with a message, as in `(data, ctx) => isSlug(data) || ctx.reject({ message: "Use lowercase letters and dashes." })`, isn't one of those: it's written as its test and its message, and fails as a built-in check does.

## Production builds

In development and tests, validators check at runtime what the build verified, so a program the build couldn't fully see fails where it would otherwise misbehave:

- [`freeze`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#freeze): writing to a validator or its members throws in strict mode code.
- [`creationChecks`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#creationchecks): a factory checks at creation that each Type, Module, Scope and Generic it receives is the one the build read, as a module mock or hot reload could replace it, and that what it reads through an import cycle is already set.
- [`config`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#configuration): the first validator created fixes the configuration, so a `configure()` the build didn't find throws.

A production build leaves these out, as `freeze: false`, `creationChecks: "none"` and `config: false`, unless an option or `ark.json` sets one. A factory still checks each function another module supplies, and each value its definition read off an object or array the program could change. A build reading the bundle whole refuses a definition where it sees the write. A write it can't see, like one by a module loaded with `require()`, throws as the validator is created, naming the value. A build written for size, as `optimize: "size"` or [`"smallest"`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#presets) sets, checks as much and leaves the names out of the bundle, so it throws `A value a validator reads is 4, but was precompiled as 3`: build with another `optimize` to read which. A list or enum read whole, like `Object.values(Plan.Enum)`, is checked by a digest of its keys and values, so the validator doesn't name each again. What counts as production:

- Vite's `build` command, outside Vitest
- webpack, Rspack and Rsbuild in `production` mode, their default
- Farm in `production` mode, as `farm build` sets it
- esbuild and `Bun.build` with `"production"` among their `conditions`
- `arktype-precompile --emit`, unless `NODE_ENV` is set to something else
- Turbopack, the Node and Bun drivers, `arktype-precompile --check` and the ESLint rule where `NODE_ENV` is `production`, as `next build` sets it

Rollup and Rolldown builds keep the checks unless set.

## ark.json

The plugin, the Node and Bun drivers, Turbopack, `arktype-precompile` and the ESLint rule each read `ark.json` beside the nearest `package.json` to `cwd`, so each builds with the same options:

```json
{
	"$schema": "./node_modules/@ark/aot/ark.schema.json",
	"precompile": {
		"preset": "smallest",
		"config": "./src/config.ts"
	}
}
```

It takes each option but `cwd`, `inline` and `declare`, and resolves `config`, `tsconfig` and each key of [`schemas`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#strategies-and-schemas) against its own directory. An option given in a call overrides it, `members`, `dependencies`, `strategies` and `schemas` key by key, and a preset fills in only what neither sets. A dependency's `ark.json` isn't read, as the program's options build every package. The build reads the file as it starts, and fails on an option it sets wrongly, naming the file and key:

```
/app/ark.json: precompile.optimize must be "size" or "speed" (was "small")
```

The same settings can go under an `"ark"` key in that `package.json` instead, resolved against its directory:

```json
{
	"name": "my-app",
	"ark": {
		"precompile": { "config": "./src/config.ts" }
	}
}
```

A watch build or dev server reads them again as they change, so a build never mixes modules written under two settings. Rollup and Vite build every module anew under the new ones, Vite's dev server restarting to, unless they change what a Vite build's config was given, like `runtime`. That, and any change under webpack, Rspack, Rolldown, esbuild or Turbopack, fails each build until you restore them or restart it, naming the restart.

Where `package.json` sets `"ark.precompile"` and an `ark.json` is beside it, the build fails, naming both, so keep one. A library's `package.json` also sets `"aot": true` under `"ark"` to [opt in](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#libraries), which is unrelated to `"precompile"`, how the program reading the file builds, so it may build with an `ark.json` beside it.

## Settings

### errors

`errors: "first"` stops each validation at the first issue it finds and returns it alone. Which of the data's issues that is isn't promised: the validator looks for whichever is cheapest to find, which may not be the one arktype finds first. `errors: "none"` returns errors holding one root issue with the code `"predicate"` and the message `is invalid`, so no check's description or message ships. It asks a narrow once, so one answering false and then true fails where arktype, asking again for its errors, returns the data. Those errors have every member other errors do, so `assert` and `throw()` throw a `TraversalError` saying `is invalid`, whose `arkErrors` are the errors.

The plugin, the Node and Bun drivers and the Turbopack loader, through [the alias Setup names](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#next), resolve `arktype/schema/runtime` to `arktype/schema/runtime/none` under `errors: "none"`, and a module importing any other `arktype/schema` entry, or a runtime island, fails the build.

The values are [arktype's `errors`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#errors) option's, and a program that also configures it must configure the same value.

### mutatesInput

`mutatesInput: true` or `"always"` writes what a validation transforms into its input and returns it, as [arktype's option](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#mutatesinput) does. A program that also configures it must configure the same value.

### members

`members` decides what a validator has besides validating. `assert`, `meta`, `~standard`, `methods` (`traverse()`, `from()` and `toString()`) and `withContext` default to true. A dropped one reads `undefined`, and the build fails where it sees the program read one, like `User.assert(data)` or `String(User)`.

`expression`, `description`, `json`, `toJSON`, `toJsonSchema` and `~standard.jsonSchema`, the introspection members, are each baked into the validators the build sees code read it off, and set true or false, into every validator or none. Where it can't see one, `String(User)` without `expression` is `"Type"`, and another reads `undefined`. Where `arktype/runtime` resolves under the [`"development"` condition](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/validators#errors), the read is still `undefined`, so code testing whether a validator has it, like a Standard Schema library asking whether `"jsonSchema" in schema["~standard"]`, behaves as it does in production, but the first read of each member also warns, naming the member and the setting, unless the validator lacks `methods`:

```
toJsonSchema isn't precompiled: set members["toJsonSchema"] true in the precompile options
```

The build follows each validator from its definition to the code reading it: through bindings, calls, returns, callbacks, `await` and the objects and arrays holding it, into its dependencies' functions, like the MCP SDK's `registerTool`. A validator stored at an object's key, as a library registering one does, is followed to each read of that key by name in the package storing it, the packages depending on that one and the program. A branch a check of what the validator is rules out, like `schema["~standard"].vendor === "zod"`, isn't followed, and neither are the helpers tsc and SWC declare in each module they emit as CommonJS, like `__createBinding` and `_interop_require_wildcard`, which read a module's exports by key and no object a program stores a validator in. Any other read of a key the code doesn't name, like `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptors(o)` in the program or a workspace package, may read the key a validator is stored at, so the build loses track of each stored one there: in a large app, where some module does, set `members` for the validators a form or router library is passed. So a validator only validated bakes none, and one hono-openapi converts bakes each, as it loses track in hono-openapi's converter. So does one an MCP tool's `inputSchema` holds, as the SDK reads objects at keys it doesn't name, any of which may hold it.

Where it loses track of a validator, it bakes each introspection member into it: where it's passed to a function the build can't resolve, like a method of an object a dependency returns, read at a computed key or as a whole, by a spread or `Object.assign`, held by a `Map` or the global object, exported by a CommonJS module, as `exports.User = User`, or followed along more paths than the build follows. A [production bundle](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#prune) warns once, naming the first validator, where it lost track and the fix:

```
precompile: baking each introspection member into the validator at src/router.ts:9:14, because src/router.ts:24:10 passes it to t.procedure.input, which the build can't follow. Set expression, description, json, toJSON, toJsonSchema and ~standard.jsonSchema in members, each false where no code reads it, to build without this warning.
```

It doesn't warn where it lost track only past a dependency's read at a key that dependency doesn't name, as in the MCP SDK, since every program using it would warn.

A production bundle reads every module, so it follows a validator a module exports to its importers. One an entry, or a module a dependency imports, exports may be read by code outside the bundle, so the build bakes nothing for that code. A build reading one module at a time, like webpack, Rspack and Turbopack where they don't [prune](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#prune), the Node and Bun drivers and `arktype-precompile --emit`, follows a validator through its module and into its dependencies. Each module importing one follows what it does with it the same way, and bakes what that reads into it where it's read, each introspection member where it loses track, as where it passes it to `registerTool`. One a module stores at a key, or exports inside an object, bakes each where it's created, as code in another module may read it. A [frozen](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#freeze) validator takes nothing from its importers, so in development, as on a dev server, one a module exports bakes each where it's created. So a validator has at least what a production bundle bakes it in development, and a production build reading one module at a time bakes what a module reads of it there. A read the build doesn't transform, like one outside the bundle reading an entry's export, throws in production alone. A build reading one module at a time doesn't transform a module that loads its validators only by `require()`, so nothing it reads of them is baked: set each member it reads true.

Keep `assert` or `~standard` on validators you pass to a library. tRPC, for one, calls a validator that has neither as a plain parse function, so it passes on the errors the validator returns as if they were the parsed input.

Each introspection member is baked as arktype returns it under the program's configuration. `toJsonSchema()` then takes a `target` whose schema is baked, which is each where `members` sets `toJsonSchema`, and a `fallback` where `~standard.jsonSchema` is baked with it or `members` sets it: the build records what arktype hands each handler of a fallback and does with what it returns, and the validator does the same with the handlers a call passes. So hono-openapi, which passes a fallback for every Type, and oRPC's converter, which passes one for a `Date`, get what arktype returns, for a Type holding a `Date`, a morph or a `.narrow()` too. Other options throw, as does a fallback where arktype reads what it returns other than to write a union, as for a `Date` with keys of its own. A JSON Schema the build can't bake throws where it's read.

```ts
precompile.vite({
	members: { assert: false, toJsonSchema: true, "~standard.jsonSchema": true }
})
```

### optimize and optimizeErrors

`optimize: "size"` writes validators for size rather than speed. With detailed errors, each node becomes a call to one of a few small runtime checkers, like `props({ name: ... })`, each describing what it checks from its rule, so the build writes a description only where yours differs, and each site creates its validator in place. A Type configured with a `message`, like a form's field, is the checker of what it checks, wrapped to say that message at each of its sites and where its key is missing, so fields checking the same thing share one checker and each holds only its own text. A module whose Types are too few to pay for the checkers' runtime has its nodes compiled instead. Validators are then slower, most where one calls several others in turn. Writing a default copies data as other builds do, except that an instance of any native class, not only those arktype lists, is written in place.

`optimizeErrors` writes errors the same way, and is `optimize` unless set. Errors written for speed [find their issues once they're read](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#valid-and-invalid-data), so a failing call whose errors nothing reads costs little more than its check. Errors written for size are the smallest a build can return, find their issues as a call fails, and are slower to read, but they have the same `count`, `issues`, `summary`, `throw()`, `toJSON()` and `toString()` as other errors, and `instanceof type.errors` recognizes them.

The build loads `arktype/schema/runtime/lean` in place of `arktype/schema/runtime` for them, or `arktype/schema/runtime/none-lean` with `errors: "none"`, and a runtime island fails the build, as under [`errors: "none"`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#errors).

### strategies and schemas

`optimize` is one choice for a whole build. `schemas` makes it for each definition: it maps a module, or one of a module's declarations, to the name of a strategy, and the build writes each validator as its strategy says. Every build has two strategies: `"fastest"` writes a validator as `optimize: "speed"` does, and `"smallest"` as `optimize: "size"` does. A definition no key matches is written as the build's own `optimize` or preset says. So a bundle that validates forms and also validates on a hot path can build `"smallest"` and compile that path alone:

```ts
precompile.vite({
	preset: "smallest",
	schemas: {
		// each Type a request handler validates with
		"src/server/**": "fastest",
		// one declaration of a module
		"src/schemas/money.ts#Money": "fastest"
	}
})
```

A build left compiled writes the Types of its forms as checkers the other way around:

```json
{
	"precompile": {
		"schemas": { "src/forms/**": "smallest" }
	}
}
```

A key is a path from [`cwd`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#cwd), or from its own directory in `ark.json`, written with `/`. In it, `*` stands for any part of a name, `**` for any directories, `?` for one character and `{a,b}` for either, and a directory stands for every module under it. Brackets are the path's own, as in a route like `"app/users/[id]/page.tsx"`. A `#` and a name after the path choose for one of the module's top-level declarations, by its own name, a name it's exported under, or `default`, and so for each definition inside it.

`strategies` names your own, each for what you'd change at once:

```ts
precompile.vite({
	strategies: {
		hot: { optimize: "speed" },
		cold: { optimize: "size" }
	},
	schemas: {
		"src/server/**": "hot",
		"src/forms/**": "cold"
	}
})
```

A strategy sets `optimize` alone, and one that sets nothing writes as the build's own does. `"fastest"` and `"smallest"` can't be defined again. Every other option stays the build's: `optimizeErrors`, which follows the build's own `optimize` unless set, `errors`, `members`, `lazy` and the rest are the same for each validator.

A marker chooses for the statement or expression after it, as [`// @ark-runtime`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands) does, so a choice can stay beside its definition:

```ts
// @ark-strategy fastest // checked on every request
export const Money = type({ amount: "number > 0", currency: "string == 3" })
```

A second `//` starts a reason the build ignores. Without one, what follows the marker is the strategy's name, so a misspelled one fails the build.

Where more than one chooses for a definition, the most specific does: a key naming its declaration, then a marker, then a key naming its module's path, the module's own over its directory's, then a glob, and of two globs the one writing more of the path before its first wildcard. Two globs writing as much that choose otherwise fail the build, naming both and the module. What chooses for a definition overrides `optimize`, a preset and the size a build [chooses for a browser's bundle](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#choosing-smallest), each of which decides only what nothing chose for. That build's estimate weighs only the validators nothing chose for, too.

A strategy writes a definition's whole validator, the Types it composes included, whatever their own definitions are written as.
