With `Money` written `"fastest"` and a form's `Order` holding it written `"smallest"`, `Money`'s checks are written twice: compiled for `Money`, and as checkers within `Order`. A bundle with validators of both kinds also holds what each reads of the runtime. So choosing costs size where Types written differently compose each other, and on a few Types it can cost more than it saves.

Two definitions of one Type, like `type({ id: "string" })` written twice, are one validator, as they're one Type to arktype. Within a module it's written as the fastest of their strategies, and across modules as the definition created first is.

A [production bundle](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#prune) written as one chunk declares in one function the units the build's own options compile, and not those a key or marker compiles. With [`lazy: false`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#lazy), it declares the units written for size in one module, those of the build's own options apart from those a key or marker chose. `lazy` is the build's for every validator, so a compiled build choosing `"smallest"` for its forms writes them smaller with `lazy: false`, as the `"smallest"` preset sets.

The build fails on a name that isn't a strategy, a key matching no file and a key naming a declaration that holds no definition, each naming the nearest that would do, and on a key naming or a marker on a definition [`// @ark-runtime`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands) leaves to arktype. Where `schemas` has a key, `arktype-precompile --check` prints after each definition what it's written with and what chose that, and fails a key whose modules define nothing:

```
src/forms/order.ts:4:22  accepted  optimize: "size"
src/server/money.ts:3:22  accepted  fastest by schemas["src/server/**"]
```

### jsonInput

`jsonInput: true` trusts each object a validator checks to be plain data, as `JSON.parse` returns: it has no non-enumerable own key and inherits no key but those `Object.prototype` has. A Type rejecting undeclared keys then counts an object's keys, as most validators do, rather than checking each against the declared ones.

On an object whose prototype is `Object.prototype`, the validator counts the keys `for...in` reaches, and where that's the number of declared keys the object holds, it holds no undeclared key. Otherwise, the validator checks each key as without `jsonInput`, and a validation that fails reports each undeclared key. A Type declaring a key `Object.prototype` has, like `toString`, a symbol key, an index signature or a tuple is checked key by key, as is every Type in an `optimize: "size"` build with detailed errors whose nodes are written as calls to runtime checkers rather than compiled. Types deleting undeclared keys are unaffected.

Data it doesn't trust to be plain can pass with an undeclared key. A declared key held as a non-enumerable property isn't counted, so an undeclared key passes in its place:

```ts
const User = type({ "+": "reject", name: "string" })
const data = Object.defineProperty({ extra: 1 }, "name", { value: "Ada" })
// passes with jsonInput: true, and fails "extra must be removed" without it
User(data)
```

An instance of a class, or any object whose prototype isn't `Object.prototype`, is checked key by key, so a getter its class declares can't stand in for a key.

### bakedLimit

A site whose baked introspection members total more than `bakedLimit` characters, 1 MB by default, fails the build naming the members and their sizes: read fewer of its members, or leave it to arktype with `// @ark-runtime` or `runtime: "arktype"`. What `json` and a JSON Schema repeat counts once, as it's written once however many Types reuse it, and each read of a JSON Schema still assembles objects of its own.

### freeze

`freeze: false`, the default in a [production build](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#production-builds), leaves validators and their members unfrozen. Otherwise, writing to one throws in strict mode code.

### lazy

`lazy: false` creates each validator as its module loads rather than where it's first read, so an error creating one throws on import.

### creationChecks

`creationChecks` decides what a factory checks at creation of what it receives: `"types"` (the default) checks each Type, Module, Scope and Generic is the one the build read, `"helpers"` (the default under Vitest, `node --test` and `bun test`) each static helper too, and `"none"` (the default in a [production build](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#production-builds)) only those holding functions, so a module mock replacing any other goes unnoticed.

### prune

A [production](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#production-builds) bundle reads every module its entries reach before it precompiles one, and leaves out of its validators each member of [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) no read needs. A validator only called, or read for `.allows`, keeps neither `assert`, `meta`, `~standard` nor `methods`, and one read as `User.assert(data)` keeps `assert`. It follows a validator into the code it's passed to as it does for the introspection members, so one Hono's `sValidator` holds keeps `~standard`, which it validates through, and nothing else. One an MCP tool's `inputSchema` holds keeps each, without a warning, as where it bakes each introspection member. With `lazy: false`, as `"smallest"` sets, it also writes a checker that only one validator reads where that validator is created, rather than as a declaration of its own, and, in a bundle of several chunks, declares the units many of its modules read in one module, and those the same modules reach in one module each, so a bundler that copies a small module into each chunk reading it, as webpack and Rspack do, holds them once. A long call to the runtime such a module writes more than once is declared there once, and each module declares only what the program's validators read of it.

A bundle written as one chunk, an esbuild build with one entry and neither `splitting` nor `inject`, or a Rollup, Rolldown, Vite, webpack or Rspack build with one entry that imports nothing dynamically, also declares the units its validators share in one function wherever that's smaller, which V8 inlines as it does a factory's parameters. Built for size, it declares them in one module instead, each validator among them. A module the build didn't read as the bundle holds it, like a file changed after the build read it or precompiled code another plugin loads, fails the build where it reads one of those units.

The build leaves a member wherever it can't prove no code reads it:

- an entry, or a module a dependency imports, exports a validator or a module holding one
- the build loses track of a validator, as [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) lists for the introspection members, or code it can't see may read an object holding one, like a function it can't resolve that it's passed to
- a module is imported dynamically, through `require` or `import.meta.glob()`, or holds a Scope
- a module reads an `import.meta` property other than `env`, `hot`, `webpackHot`, `url`, `resolve`, `dirname`, `filename` and the flags Nuxt defines, like `client` and `dev`
- an esbuild bundle holds a module it can't read, like a Vue component
- a `define` names a binding rather than a literal or a global, as `READ: "local.expression"` does, since no module's text holds the code it writes

A Vite, Rollup or Rolldown build reads each module as the bundler loads it, so it reads a component as its framework's plugin compiles it, like a Svelte, Vue or Astro component or an MDX page, and a virtual module as the plugin writing it does. A webpack or Rspack build reads its modules once it has built them as they are, so it reads what its resolver, aliases and loaders make of them, and what Next.js's generated entries import, then builds again those it writes. It reads each module Next.js's `experimental.optimizePackageImports` builds a listed package's entry as, one for each set of names imported from it, as that entry's file. An `import()` or `require()` of a computed specifier, like ``import(`./icons/${name}`)``, loads one of the modules the bundler built for the files it can name, so the build keeps each member only where one of those exports a validator. Each of Next.js's compilers prunes by its own modules. A member set true is always kept.

Where it can't prune, the build warns once, in the bundler's own warnings, naming the first module that kept it from pruning and how, and the fix. Where it can't read every module the bundle holds, it builds as `prune: false` does:

```
prune: off, because src/routes.ts:3:1 reads import.meta.glob, which may load modules it can't name, so the build keeps every member of its validators. Set prune: false to build them whole without this warning.
```

Where it reads them all but not what a read of its validators needs, it keeps each member `members` leaves to it, and still writes what else pruning does:

```
prune: keeping assert, meta, ~standard, methods and withContext, because src/index.ts exports User, which code outside the bundle may read. Set assert, meta, ~standard, methods and withContext in members, each true where code reads it, like ~standard where a library validates with it, else false, to build without this warning.
```

Setting each in `members` clears it, as the build then has no member left to decide. Where `NODE_ENV` is `production`, `arktype-precompile --check` prints the same warning for a bundle of the files it checks, but tests, stories and configs. It follows relative imports of scripts alone and reads no file as an entry, so it misses what an alias, a virtual module, a component or an entry's exports lead to.

Vite, Rollup, Rolldown, esbuild, webpack and Rspack bundles and `next build` with Turbopack prune, esbuild only where this plugin is the last, so no plugin loads a module after it reads it. `prune: true` also prunes a Rollup, Rolldown, esbuild, webpack or Rspack bundle that isn't for production, which the build can't tell. The Node and Bun drivers and `arktype-precompile --emit` build every validator whole, and fail with `prune: true`, set in their options or `ark.json`, as does an esbuild build where a plugin follows this one. `next dev` builds them whole under any setting.

A Vite, Rollup or Rolldown build reads each module from its file, then reads the bundle again as it was built, each module as the plugins ahead of this one wrote it and as the transforms after this one's left it, and fails only where the built bundle reads what it left out, a member or more of a call's errors, naming the read. A plugin that rewrites a module without adding a read, like a Babel plugin or TanStack Router's code splitting, changes nothing, listed ahead of this one or after it. One that adds a read of a validator fails the build wherever it's listed, as no order of plugins has the build keep what such a read needs. Where its transform runs after this one's, as one listed after `precompile.vite()` or one without `enforce: "pre"` does, the build names the module, the read and each plugin whose transform follows this one's, and the members that, set true, keep all the read needs:

```
vite-plugin-macros transformed src/form.ts after arktype's plugin read it, and the program as built reads what the build left out of its validators: a module reads assert of a validator. Set assert true in members, or prune: false to build each validator whole.
```

Where no member does, as for a validator the added code passes on, it names `prune: false` alone. A plugin following this one that changes the code this one wrote for a module's validators fails the build too, as the build can't tell what the result reads of them: give it `enforce: "pre"` and list it ahead of `precompile.vite()`, or set `prune: false`. The build reads no chunk as an output plugin's `renderChunk` or `generateBundle` writes it, so set `members` for a read one of those adds.

An esbuild build reads each module as it loads it, and fails where another plugin loaded one. A webpack or Rspack build reads a module as it reached the plugin, a loader ahead's work included, then reads each module again as the loaders after it built it, and fails where that reads a member it left out, naming the module, the read and the loaders. Each import a loader after it adds keeps every member of what that import reaches. Where it can't read a module, it builds as `prune: false` does, as no module was written yet. `prune: false` builds every validator whole, each unit a module of its own.

### dependencies

`dependencies` decides how the build treats a package that imports arktype but doesn't [opt in](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#libraries), which otherwise fails it. `"aot"` precompiles the package as if it opted in, for one whose Types are static, like t3-env's `presets-arktype`. `"arktype"` runs it on arktype, as a [runtime island](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands) runs, for one creating Types from values it reads as it runs, like `drizzle-arktype`:

```json
{
	"precompile": {
		"dependencies": {
			"@t3-oss/env-core": "aot",
			"drizzle-arktype": "arktype"
		}
	}
}
```

A [workspace package](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#frameworks), which the build precompiles with the program, runs on arktype too where `"arktype"` names it, by the name its `package.json` declares, as its modules resolve to its own directory rather than to `node_modules`.

A package run on arktype ships arktype's parser for the Types it creates, under the program's configuration. Its errors are instances of `type.errors`, as a precompiled validator's are, and its Types are Standard Schemas, so the rest of the program reads them as it reads any. `"arktype"` fails the build with `errors: "none"` or `optimizeErrors: "size"`, whose errors are a class of their own, and with Turbopack or Bun's runtime plugin, which replace arktype for every importer. A name the program can't resolve fails the build.

A package precompiled with `"aot"` is read as the program is, so a value it returns that the build can't tell from a Type is checked where it's read: `JSON.stringify(env)` on t3-env's result fails as reading `toJSON`, unless `env` is annotated with its type.

### allowUnsafe

`allowUnsafe: true` (`--allow-unsafe` for `--check`) reports as warnings the problems that may throw at runtime but that a build can still write output for: a dependency that imports arktype or ships precompiled validators, a module the build can't precompile importing arktype, a read off an import it can't resolve, an import that loads a Type before the config module, a Turbopack alias for `arktype/schema/runtime` other than `@ark/aot/turbopack/runtime`, a package the build leaves external that loads arktype beside the runtime, and a definition that throws a ParseError. Each fails the build otherwise. It applies with `runtime: "arktype"` too, where a ParseError and a dependency shipping precompiled validators fail the build and the rest are warnings anyway.

### checker

`checker` chooses the TypeScript that [declarations](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#declarations) read the program with: `"tsjs"` for the compiler API of TypeScript 5.5 to 6, or `"tsgo"` or `"tsrs"` for TypeScript 7.1 or later's native API. It defaults to the TypeScript installed, preferring tsrs to tsgo where its binary is installed, and before 7.1 (or with `"tsjs"` under TypeScript 7) reads `typescript-6` installed beside it (`npm i -D typescript-6@npm:typescript@6`).

### conditions and tsconfig

`conditions` and `tsconfig` set the export conditions and the tsconfig whose `paths` the build resolves imports with.

### cwd

`cwd` is the directory the build finds [`ark.json`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#arkjson) and the packages that [opt in](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#libraries) from, and resolves a relative `config` against. The plugin defaults it to the bundler's root: Vite's `root`, webpack's and Rspack's `context` and esbuild's `absWorkingDir`. Other hosts default it to the current directory.

## Configuration

A program that calls `configure()` does so once, in a module imported before any that defines a Type, and names it as the build's `config`:

```ts
import { configure } from "arktype/config"

configure({
	onUndeclaredKey: "delete",
	onFail: errors => errors.throw()
})
```

```ts
precompile.vite({ config: "./config.ts" })
```

The build evaluates the argument, which must be static, and precompiles every definition under it. `onFail` can be any function.

A `message`, `expected` or `actual` configured for a code, or on a Type with `.configure()` or its meta, as a string or a function, is written as arktype writes it. What a standalone validator can't write fails the build, each with its fix:

- a locale
- a function writing a union's or a discriminated union's text, which arktype passes each branch's errors: configure the text as a string
- text a Scope configures for a code: configure it with `configure()`, or on each Type with `.configure()`
- `predicate` text from `configure()` where a narrow or morph raises the error: pass the text to `ctx.reject()`

The build fails where a module that creates a Type is imported before the config module, and the runtime throws if `configure()` runs after it creates its first validator, runs again with other values, or receives other values than the build read. Run again with the same values, as when a test runner resets its modules and the config module runs again, it changes nothing, as arktype's does.

`config: false`, the default in a [production build](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#production-builds), says the program never calls `configure()`, so the build fails wherever it does. A program that calls it names its module as `config`, which overrides the default.

A program configuring `errors` or `mutatesInput` builds with the same value. Configured otherwise by `configure()`, the build fails once, at the call, and for a Scope, at each definition whose Types it configures. The build also fails where `configure()` sets either without the config module importing `arktype/errors` or `arktype/mutatesInput`, as arktype throws creating a Type without it.

# Size at scale

> What each Type adds to a bundle, dynamic and precompiled, and where each is the smaller.

A bundle pays for validation twice: once for the library, and again for each Type. ArkType's two modes split that differently.

- **Dynamic** arktype ships its parser and compiler, a fixed cost, and each Type adds only its definition.
- **Precompiled**, neither ships, so the fixed cost is small, and each Type adds its validator: checks compiled for it by default, or with [`preset: "smallest"`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#choosing-smallest), what shared checkers read.

So which is smaller depends on how many Types a bundle holds, and on what they hold. This page measures both, with Valibot and Zod beside them, from 1 to 5,000 Types.

## What's measured

Each app is modules of 25 Types, no two alike, written the same way in each library and bundled whole by esbuild 0.25.10, tree-shaken and minified, with ArkType 3.0.0-beta.1 (1718e5066), Valibot 1.5.0 and Zod 4.6.7. Every number is the mean of 3 apps generated from different seeds.

What's bundled is an app, not a package of schemas. It exports one function, which takes a Type's name and some input and runs that Type's handler: validate the input, then return the data or the text of what's wrong with it, as a route or a form's submit does. Each library does that in its own words:

| Library | Validates with | Reads what's wrong with |
| - | - | - |
| ArkType | `Contact(input)` | `errors.summary` |
| Valibot | `v.safeParse(Contact, input)` | `v.summarize(issues)` |
| Zod | `Contact.safeParse(input)` | `z.prettifyError(error)` |
| Zod Mini | `z.safeParse(Contact, input)` | `z.prettifyError(error)` |

Nothing outside the bundle can read a Type, so each library ships what those two need and no more. A precompiled build leaves out the parts of a validator no handler reads, like `assert` and its Standard Schema interface. Valibot leaves out the functions no handler calls, like `parse`. Zod's schemas are classes, which keep their methods, and Zod Mini's keep their parsing whichever function runs it. A bundle that exports its Types instead, as a package of schemas does, keeps all of each one: whoever imports it might read any of it.

Each app is written twice:

- **Models** are objects of ids, bounded strings, formats, integers, enums, optional keys, defaults, arrays, references to each other and discriminated unions, as an API's requests and responses are. None has a message or a function of its own.
- **Forms** are the same Types, where 35% of their fields that aren't references or arrays have a message of their own and 25% of their plain strings and integers a narrow, about 1.8 messages and 0.5 narrows a Type. Those are the rates we counted in a production frontend's forms.

```ts
import { type } from "arktype"

const isTrimmed = (s: string) => s === s.trim()

const Contact = type({
	// a message of its own
	email: type("string.email").configure({ message: "Enter your work email." }),
	// a narrow, with its message
	name: type("1 <= string <= 100").narrow(
		(value, ctx) =>
			isTrimmed(value) ||
			ctx.reject({ message: "Name can't start or end with a space." })
	)
})
```

26% of an app's modules, spread evenly from where its seed starts them, hold the handlers of the Types they define, and the rest have theirs in a module that imports the Types. That's how that frontend is laid out: code in the module declaring a Type uses 55 of its 210 Types, and in 42 of the 46 files with such a Type, that's every Type the file declares. Which of the two a handler is in moves no build's gzipped bundle by more than 0.5%.

The default build here is the compiled one a server gets. Building for a browser, it [writes its validators for size](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#choosing-smallest) once they'd outweigh arktype.

[Benchmarks](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/benchmarks#rerun-them) has how to rerun every number on this page.

## Models

| Types | "smallest" | Default | Dynamic | Valibot | Zod | Zod Mini |
| - | - | - | - | - | - | - |
| 1 | 1.3 KB | 1.4 KB | 101 KB | 1.8 KB | 25.8 KB | 6.4 KB |
| 10 | 3.2 KB | 4.3 KB | 102 KB | 3.4 KB | 28.2 KB | 10.4 KB |
| 50 | 5.4 KB | 11.2 KB | 104 KB | 5.5 KB | 30.2 KB | 12.5 KB |
| 100 | 7.4 KB | 19.0 KB | 106 KB | 7.6 KB | 32.2 KB | 14.6 KB |
| 250 | 12.8 KB | 39.9 KB | 112 KB | 13.3 KB | 37.8 KB | 20.4 KB |
| 500 | 21.4 KB | 73.7 KB | 122 KB | 22.9 KB | 47.1 KB | 30.0 KB |
| 1,000 | 38.6 KB | 140 KB | 142 KB | 42.0 KB | 65.7 KB | 48.8 KB |
| 2,500 | 88.6 KB | 335 KB | 201 KB | 99.0 KB | 121 KB | 105 KB |
| 5,000 | 172 KB | 659 KB | 300 KB | 195 KB | 214 KB | 201 KB |

With one Type of a model, the "smallest" build gzips to 1.3 KB and the default build to 1.4 KB, where dynamic arktype is 101 KB, Valibot 1.8 KB, Zod Mini 6.4 KB and Zod 25.8 KB.

Against Valibot on models, "smallest" gzips smaller at every count measured from 10 to 5,000 Types, by 2.7% to 12%. In raw bytes it's smaller at every count measured from 10 to 5,000 Types, by 22% to 37%.

On models, "smallest" gzips smaller at every count measured, and each Type adds 34.1 B to it and 39.6 B to dynamic arktype, so more Types only widen its lead. The default build gzips smaller until about 1,000 Types, as each Type adds 133 B to it and 39.6 B to dynamic arktype: it's the smaller at 1,000 and the larger at 2,500, and the seeds' lines cross between 1,000 and 1,000.

On forms, "smallest" gzips smaller at every count measured, and each Type adds 53.6 B to it and 63.5 B to dynamic arktype, so more Types only widen its lead. In raw bytes it's smaller at every count measured, and each Type adds 237 B to it and 411 B to dynamic arktype, so more Types only widen its lead. The default build gzips smaller until about 690 Types, as each Type adds 191 B to it and 63.5 B to dynamic arktype: it's the smaller at 500 and the larger at 1,000, and the seeds' lines cross between 670 and 700.

## What each Type adds

A bundle's bytes are close to a line: what it costs before its first Type, then the same again for each one. On models:

| Build | Fixed, gzip | Each Type, gzip | Fixed, raw | Each Type, raw |
| - | - | - | - | - |
| ArkType precompiled, "smallest" | 4.1 KB | 34.1 B (33.8 to 34.3) | 8.2 KB | 130 B (128 to 131) |
| ArkType precompiled, default | 5.9 KB | 133 B (130 to 137) | 18.5 KB | 906 B (887 to 929) |
| ArkType dynamic | 102 KB | 39.6 B (39.4 to 40.0) | 301 KB | 234 B (233 to 237) |
| Valibot | 3.8 KB | 38.2 B (37.8 to 38.6) | 8.0 KB | 209 B (208 to 211) |
| Zod | 28.5 KB | 37.1 B (36.9 to 37.5) | 93.2 KB | 214 B (213 to 217) |
| Zod Mini | 10.8 KB | 38.0 B (37.7 to 38.4) | 30.4 KB | 204 B (203 to 207) |

On forms:

| Build | Fixed, gzip | Each Type, gzip | Fixed, raw | Each Type, raw |
| - | - | - | - | - |
| ArkType precompiled, "smallest" | 4.8 KB | 53.6 B (53.2 to 54.2) | 8.9 KB | 237 B (236 to 241) |
| ArkType precompiled, default | 10.3 KB | 191 B (188 to 196) | 25.1 KB | 1,502 B (1,479 to 1,539) |
| ArkType dynamic | 102 KB | 63.5 B (63.0 to 64.2) | 299 KB | 411 B (407 to 416) |
| Valibot | 4.1 KB | 57.8 B (57.4 to 58.6) | 7.2 KB | 323 B (320 to 327) |
| Zod | 28.5 KB | 58.6 B (58.1 to 59.4) | 91.2 KB | 362 B (358 to 368) |
| Zod Mini | 11.1 KB | 59.7 B (59.3 to 60.5) | 29.3 KB | 349 B (346 to 355) |

Each line is fitted to the counts from 100 Types up, where growth is steady, and is within 5.7% of every mean it's fitted to. The range after each Type's bytes is the seeds', each fitted alone.

## What a message and a narrow cost

Forms differ from models by their messages and narrows, so an app with only one of the two says what each adds:

| Build | A message, gzip | A message, raw | A narrow, gzip | A narrow, raw |
| - | - | - | - | - |
| ArkType precompiled, "smallest" | 7.4 B | 39.2 B | 12.4 B | 63.4 B |
| ArkType precompiled, default | 19.2 B | 193 B | 38.6 B | 417 B |
| ArkType dynamic | 9.4 B | 69.3 B | 14.5 B | 95.3 B |
| Valibot | 7.8 B | 45.4 B | 11.6 B | 59.5 B |
| Zod | 8.7 B | 63.1 B | 11.8 B | 64.0 B |
| Zod Mini | 8.9 B | 63.1 B | 11.8 B | 60.2 B |

At 5,000 Types, a message adds 7.4 B gzipped to a "smallest" bundle and 7.8 B to Valibot's, and a narrow adds 12.4 B and 11.6 B.

With messages alone, "smallest" gzips smaller at every count measured from 10 to 5,000 Types, by 0.4% to 10%. With narrows alone, it gzips smaller at 10 Types, by 2.3% to 4.4%; within 1.4% either way at 50 to 100 Types; smaller at 250 to 5,000 Types, by 1.4% to 9.6%.

At 5,000 Types, a message costs "smallest" no more than it costs Valibot, so of the two only narrows can cost it its lead: taking them alone, a "smallest" bundle gzips smaller than Valibot's while it has fewer than about 6.0 narrows a Type.

## Where each is smaller

Each count is where the lines between the two measured counts around it meet. On models:

| Build | Against | Gzip | Raw |
| - | - | - | - |
| "smallest" | Valibot | smaller at every count | smaller at every count |
| "smallest" | Zod | smaller at every count | smaller at every count |
| "smallest" | Zod Mini | smaller at every count | smaller at every count |
| "smallest" | Dynamic | smaller at every count | smaller at every count |
| Default | Valibot | larger from 10 | larger from 10 |
| Default | Zod | smaller until about 230, then larger | smaller until about 110, then larger |
| Default | Zod Mini | smaller until about 61, then larger | smaller until about 29, then larger |
| Default | Dynamic | smaller until about 1,000, then larger | smaller until about 420, then larger |

On forms:

| Build | Against | Gzip | Raw |
| - | - | - | - |
| "smallest" | Valibot | smaller until about 26, larger until about 250, then smaller | smaller at every count |
| "smallest" | Zod | smaller at every count | smaller at every count |
| "smallest" | Zod Mini | smaller at every count | smaller at every count |
| "smallest" | Dynamic | smaller at every count | smaller at every count |
| Default | Valibot | larger from 10 | larger from 10 |
| Default | Zod | smaller until about 140, then larger | smaller until about 64, then larger |
| Default | Zod Mini | smaller until about 33, then larger | smaller until about 17, then larger |
| Default | Dynamic | smaller until about 690, then larger | smaller until about 250, then larger |

## Which to choose

Precompile a bundle a browser loads, with [`"smallest"`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#choosing-smallest) once it holds more than a handful of Types. Built "smallest", a bundle gzips smaller than it would shipping arktype at every count measured, on models and on forms. What it saves is arktype's fixed cost, which a page pays before it validates anything.

Keep the default build for a server and for validation on a hot path, where each validator's own compiled code is [what makes it fast](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile#speed-and-size). The default build gzips smaller than dynamic arktype until about 1,000 Types on models and until about 690 Types on forms, and in raw bytes until about 420 Types on models and until about 250 Types on forms. A bundle with both kinds of Type [chooses for each definition](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#strategies-and-schemas).

What a Type holds moves these counts more than how many there are. Gzipped, a narrow costs a "smallest" bundle 1.1x what it costs Valibot's, and a message 0.95x. If bytes are all you're choosing by, compare the rows nearest your app above.

[Dynamic vs Precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/dynamic-vs-precompiled#which-to-use) covers when to stay dynamic for reasons other than size.

# Benchmarks

> The rule the headline and the homepage's board follow, every result behind it, our own benchmark beside it and how to rerun each one.

Every number on this site comes from a benchmark in the repo. This page has the rule the headline and the homepage's board follow, every result behind it, our own benchmark beside it and the commands that rerun each one.

## The rule

The headline, the homepage's board and the tables below follow one rule, the same for validation speed, startup and bundle size.

Ranked by geometric mean across other projects' public benchmarks and valibot.dev's login form, which we wrote in each library from Valibot's code: 22 results for validation speed, 2 for startup and 2 for bundle size; the 2 startup results time creating a schema. Each category averages the largest set of results that ArkType, Zod and three more named libraries all ran, in the unit they measure, and ranks every library that ran all of them, in plain order. ArkType is its default precompiled build in all three. We name only libraries with 100k+ npm downloads a week; every place and average counts all of them.

So the headline's words mean these averages, each the first row of a table below:

- Smallest on average across valibot.dev's login form and schemabenchmarks.dev's download: 1.19 kB gzipped against Typia's 1.52 kB, 21.7% lower.
- Fastest on average across 22 results from 2 independent benchmarks: 658 CPU instructions per validation against Typia's 2,097, 68.6% lower.
- Quickest to start on average across 2 results from 2 independent benchmarks: 38 CPU instructions to create a schema against TypeBox's 4,273, 99.1% lower.

Standings as of November 19, 2026. [When each benchmark was measured](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/benchmarks#when-each-was-measured) has a date per benchmark.

Each choice has a reason:

- **Other projects' benchmarks, because we didn't write them.** Each is another project's public suite, cloned at a pinned commit and run as its authors wrote it, with ArkType added the way that suite adds a library. We chose none of their schemas, inputs or measurements. The one exception is in size: valibot.dev's login form is Valibot's code, which we wrote in each other library and size with our own script.
- **The largest set of results that five libraries share**, because a library is only compared over results it ran. A graph has five lanes: ArkType, Zod and three more libraries the site names. It averages the largest set of results that ArkType, Zod and three such libraries all ran, so every bar is over the same work. Which results those are depends on who ran what and never on what anyone scored.
- **A geometric mean**, because the results span orders of magnitude: one validates an email address, another a whole document. An arithmetic mean would be the largest result with the rest as rounding error. A geometric mean gives every result the same weight, and the ratio of two libraries' means is the mean of their ratios.
- **The unit the benchmark measures.** Speed and startup are CPU instructions, counted with `perf` while the other project's benchmark code runs. An instruction count is the same on a busy machine and on a quiet one, and close to the same on another CPU, so a number here can be checked on a machine that isn't ours. Size is bytes, minified and gzipped.
- **One build of ArkType in all three**, because a library that is fastest in one configuration and smallest in another is neither at once. Every row of every graph is the same build: precompiled with the default options, bundled for production.
- **Plain order.** A place is a library's position by its mean, lowest first, among every library that ran all of a graph's results, whether the site names it or not. Nothing counts as a tie unless two means are equal.
- **Startup counts creating a schema**, because that is what both public startup benchmarks time. A precompiled validator creates its schema when it builds and has nothing left to create when it loads; the graph shows that difference as it was measured. Importing a real app through its first validation is [our own startup benchmark](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/benchmarks#startup).

The lanes the homepage draws are ArkType, the three best-placed other libraries the site names (100k+ npm downloads a week) and Zod. Zod's other entry points, `z.compile` and Zod Mini, are in the tables below rather than in a second Zod lane.

- Every benchmark is public. We wrote 1 of the 5 for validation speed, 2 of the 4 for startup and 1 of the 4 for bundle size; the averages above leave those out. They keep valibot.dev's login form, Valibot's code, which we wrote in each library and size with our own script.
- Each of the 2 independent startup results times creating a schema, which a precompiled build does when it builds. Our own startup benchmarks time importing an app through its first validation (7 results).

A result is only as current as its last run, so each benchmark has its own date, and ArkType's rows name the commit they were measured at. Each month a job reruns the size benchmarks at each library's newest release and opens a pull request with the updated numbers for review, so a number on this site changes only by a reviewed commit.

## Our own benchmark

The rule leaves our own benchmark out of every bar, place and superlative, since we wrote it. The homepage prints two figures from it beside the bars, in units most people think in, and the sections below have all of it, including the results where another library is ahead.

### Validation speed

Nanoseconds per validation, by the clock, on one core. Each library's geometric mean over the scenarios all of them ran:

| Place | Library | ns per validation, geometric mean of 27 scenarios | Validations a second |
| - | - | - | - |
| 1st | ArkType | 123 ns | 8.1M |
| 2nd | ajv | 187 ns | 5.3M |
| 3rd | ArkType (dynamic) | 272 ns | 3.7M |
| 4th | Typia | 794 ns | 1.3M |
| 5th | Zod (compiled) | 935 ns | 1.1M |
| 6th | Valibot | 1,875 ns | 533k |
| 7th | Zod | 2,012 ns | 497k |
| 8th | TypeBox | 3,207 ns | 312k |
| 9th | Zod Mini | 4,219 ns | 237k |

Precompiled ArkType was faster than Zod 4 in all 32 scenarios of our benchmark, by a median of 15×, and faster than Zod 4's z.compile in 32 of 32, by a median of 5.3×.

It isn't the fastest at everything. On the rows that report errors for invalid data, ajv was faster on 8 of 15.

| first moltar strict | 94.6 ns | 710 ns\* | 6.26 µs | 6.29 µs | 32.4 ns | 2.29 µs\* | 2.21 µs\* | 3.14 µs\* | 716 ns | ajv | 2.9× slower |

| first items | 327 ns | 1.77 µs\* | 7.59 µs | 173 µs | 351 ns | 6.53 µs\* | 6.7 µs\* | 27.2 µs\* | 8.58 µs | ajv | 1.07× faster |
| first patterns | 3.37 µs | 3.7 µs\* | 22.1 µs | 18.4 µs | 7.5 µs | 10.5 µs\* | 17.9 µs\* | 10.2 µs\* | 7.84 µs | ajv | 2.2× faster |
| allows moltar | 3.75 ns | 3.74 ns | 4.84 ns | 98.3 ns | 14.2 ns | 136 ns | 8.01 ns | 784 ns | 461 ns | typia | 1.29× faster |
| allows moltar invalid | 3.65 ns | 3.6 ns | 4.79 ns | 98.5 ns | 29.8 ns | 239 ns | 8.52 ns | 1.01 µs | 720 ns | typia | 1.31× faster |

Median ns per call over 20 passes, each running every library in a fresh process, outputs checked against ArkType's before timing. Ties are a two-sided sign test over paired passes at p ≥ .05; ratios are of the medians, truncated. Node 25.2.1 on an Intel i7-11700 under WSL2, measured 2026-10-24 on the precompile branch (808927feb), which hasn't shipped; the numbers will be rerun on the release commit.

Zod's parse, compiled or not, and Valibot's remove undeclared keys and return a copy, where ArkType, typia, TypeBox and ajv return the input as is. The strip rows compare like for like, since every library removes them there, as do the rows that transform or default their input, where every library returns new output and ArkType's Types remove undeclared keys too. On strip moltar, ArkType is 10× faster than Zod 4, 1.38× faster than Zod 4 compiled and 36× faster than Valibot. On strip product, ArkType is 8.7× faster than Zod 4, 2× faster than Zod 4 compiled and 9.6× faster than Valibot.

Zod 4 compiled on parse tree (marked \*) runs Zod's runtime parser, since z.compile refuses recursive schemas. On the first-error rows, arms marked \* have no first-error mode and report every error.

Beyond it:

- On moltar's parseSafe benchmark, precompiled ArkType takes the fewest instructions per call, and by wall clock it was faster than each of the six libraries closest to it, Typia among them, in at least 28 of 30 paired runs.
- On apps we generated of 11 to 1,012 Types, built with esbuild, webpack and Next on Turbopack, the default build validated faster on every one than every other library measured on it (Zod 4 and Valibot on every app, z.compile and ajv on some), by 1.68x or more: nanoseconds per call over 9 paired runs on a shared machine, p ≤ 0.039.
- On ntwine's packages/shared, the schemas of an open-source app and the code that reads them, bundled with esbuild: the "smallest" preset shipped 129 KB gzipped to Zod 4's 191 KB and Zod 3's 111 KB, the version ntwine ships; it ran 0.205G instructions through its first validation to Zod 4's 0.481G and Zod 3's 0.270G; and the default build validated a thread 11.89x as fast as Zod 4 and 41.17x as fast as Zod 3, in nanoseconds per call over 9 paired runs on a shared machine, p ≤ 0.004. Zod 4 ships less through webpack (119 KB to 125 KB) and through Next on Turbopack (276 KB to 277 KB).

### Startup

From just before a fresh process imports an app's bundle to just after its first validation returns. In CPU instructions, beyond what an empty module costs to load:

| Valibot | 2.48M | 2.35M | 2.29M | 12.3M | 4.04M | 2nd |
| ajv | — | 1.87M | 1.61M | 32.9M | 4.63M | 3rd |
| Typia | — | 2.45M | 1.34M | 33.4M | 4.78M | 4th |
| Zod Mini | 11.5M | 11.4M | 10.5M | 37.0M | 16.4M | 5th |
| Zod | 44.1M | 43.7M | 54.0M | 102M | 62.3M | 6th |
| Zod (compiled) | 52.4M | 51.6M | 58.6M | 126M | 72.5M | 7th |
| TypeBox | — | 87.9M | 89.4M | 208M | 118M | 8th |

- On each of the 4 apps in our startup benchmark, precompiled ArkType's default build ran fewer instructions from import through its first validation than every other library measured on it (Valibot, Zod, Zod (compiled), Zod Mini, Typia, ajv and TypeBox), by 23.8% or more, in at least 17 of 20 paired runs on Node 24.
- From import through its first validation, the "smallest" preset ran fewer instructions than every other library on every one of those apps, by 2.8% or more through esbuild and webpack and by 2.4% or more on Turbopack, where Next's own startup is in every count, p ≤ 0.004; the default build did on 19 of them.
