| Zod (compiled) | 13.1 ms | 13.5 ms | 30.3 ms | 17.5 ms | 7th |
| TypeBox | 16.8 ms | 16.5 ms | 43.3 ms | 22.9 ms | 8th |
| ArkType (dynamic) | 31.7 ms | 29.9 ms | 50.6 ms | 36.3 ms | 9th |

Most of each of those milliseconds is Node loading a module, which every library pays alike, so the quickest are close together and their order changes from app to app and from machine to machine. Instructions count what a library adds, and a busy machine doesn't move them.

#### Against dynamic ArkType

On valid data, the precompiled build is within 6% of dynamic ArkType in 14 of 16 scenarios; it's 1.11× slower on moltar and 1.45× faster on rotating. The bigger change is everything before the first call.

| | Precompiled | Dynamic |
| - | - | - |
| Cold start, our login form app | 3.34 ms | 31.7 ms |
| Bundle gzipped, valibot.dev's login form | 0.92 kB | 98.1 kB |

Cold start is our login form app (an email and a password check), bundled and minified with esbuild: the median time for a fresh Node process to import the bundle and validate once, measured 2026-10-23 at 89510709d. Size is valibot.dev's login form, the validators and the library code they import, minified with esbuild and gzipped, at 591cc38d7.

### Bundle size

Our own apps, each bundled with esbuild as a production build, minified and gzipped:

| Library | login | moltar | shop | saas | Geometric mean of login, moltar, shop | Place |
| - | - | - | - | - | - | - |
| ajv | 0.63 kB | 0.76 kB | 8.84 kB | — | 1.61 kB | 1st |
| ArkType | 1.14 kB | 1.19 kB | 5.07 kB | 9.59 kB | 1.90 kB | 2nd |
| Valibot | 1.68 kB | 1.46 kB | 3.63 kB | 5.17 kB | 2.07 kB | 3rd |
| Typia | 1.24 kB | 1.23 kB | 16.7 kB | — | 2.94 kB | 4th |
| Zod Mini | 5.11 kB | 4.71 kB | 10.2 kB | — | 6.26 kB | 5th |
| Zod | 25.1 kB | 26.4 kB | 28.1 kB | — | 26.5 kB | 6th |
| Zod (compiled) | 32.9 kB | 34.2 kB | 35.9 kB | — | 34.3 kB | 7th |
| TypeBox | 41.9 kB | 41.9 kB | 42.9 kB | — | 42.2 kB | 8th |

On Valibot's own login form, ArkType's default build reports an error for every invalid field, with the form's messages, in a smaller bundle than Valibot: 0.92 kB gzipped against 1.56 kB.

Dynamic ArkType is 98.1 kB gzipped, minified with esbuild, up from 47.8 kB in 2.2.9, so precompile to ship less.

With the "smallest" preset, its bundle was smaller than every other library's on 20 of those 22 apps, by 31 B or more; on 11 and 46 Types through webpack with narrows, Valibot's was smaller, by up to 29 B (0.6%). It shipped less than Zod 4 on every one, by 1.18x to 10.28x. The default build, the fastest, shipped 1.25x to 2.48x what "smallest" did.

[Size at scale](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/size-at-scale) has how each build's bundle grows with the number of Types in it, and where each is the smallest.

## Build time

[Build time](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile#build-time) has what precompiling adds to a production build, a dev server and a rebuild.

## Precompiled against dynamic

A precompiled validator has to return what dynamic ArkType returns, with the same messages. These are the checks every change to the precompiler passes:

| Check | What it holds |
| - | - |
| `pnpm testDifferential` | Every Type ArkType's own test suites call, precompiled in each layout, returns what dynamic ArkType returns on every input the suites passed it. |
| `pnpm testPerturbation` | Change what the build read before the program runs, like a key, an export or a prototype: the precompiled program throws as it starts or still agrees with ArkType. |
| `pnpm testPrograms` | Generated programs agree run as written and precompiled, unchanged and under every perturbation. |
| `pnpm testPruneParity` | A production bundle missing what no code reads validates every input as one built whole does, once negative controls show the check catches a dropped check. |
| `pnpm testHistory` | Each test sees the same thing fresh, twice in one process and after a random sample of the others. |
| `pnpm testEnvironments` | A program prints the same in other time zones and locales, on Bun, Deno, Chromium and Firefox. |

In your own project, [shadow mode](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#shadow-mode) runs your tests against both and fails wherever they disagree.

## Rerun them

Clone the repo and build it once:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype
cd arktype
pnpm i && pnpm build
```

### The board

`pnpm benchExternal <suite>` clones a benchmark at the commit its published rows were counted on, installs it from its own lockfile, adds ArkType and runs it. The clones take about 4.5 GB under `ark/repo/bench/external/out/clones/`.

| Graph | Command | Needs | Takes |
| - | - | - | - |
| Validation speed | `pnpm benchExternal sb` and `pnpm benchExternal ata` | Linux, `perf`, `taskset` | about 75 minutes |
| Startup | `pnpm benchExternal sb` and `pnpm benchExternal sury` | Linux, `perf`, `taskset` | about 50 minutes |
| Bundle size | `pnpm benchExternal size` | any OS | about 2 minutes |
| All of them | `pnpm benchExternal all` | Linux, `perf`, `taskset` | about 90 minutes |

Instruction counts come from hardware counters, which `perf` reads on Linux and which most hosted CI runners and virtual machines don't expose. `NODE24` and `NODE26` name the Node 24 and 26 binaries the suites run on; without them the suites run on the Node that runs the script.

Each run writes its results to `ark/repo/bench/external/out/fresh/`. Then:

```sh
pnpm benchBoard --fresh
```

prints each graph's standings by the rule above, the published numbers beside what your checkout measured. Without `--fresh` it prints the published ones alone. It runs the code this site runs, so what it prints for the published results is what the homepage draws.

Expect every other library's bundle to match to the byte, and an instruction count to move by a few percent on another CPU or Node build while the ratios between libraries move less. ArkType's own rows are the commit you check out, and the published ones name theirs.

### Our own benchmark

| Script | What it reruns | Needs | Takes |
| - | - | - | - |
| `pnpm benchTypia` | Typia's generated validators, which the next three read | any OS | 1 to 5 minutes |
| `pnpm benchValidate` | [Validation speed](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/benchmarks#validation-speed), every scenario | any OS | about 10 minutes |
| `pnpm benchImport` | [Startup](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/benchmarks#startup) by the clock | any OS | under a minute |
| `pnpm benchSize` | [Bundle size](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/benchmarks#bundle-size) of our apps | any OS | seconds |
| `pnpm benchExternal startup` | [Startup](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/benchmarks#startup) in instructions | Linux, `perf`, `taskset` | about a minute |

`benchValidate`, `benchImport` and `benchSize` write `validate.json`, `import.json` and `size.json` to `ark/repo/bench/out/`, and `pnpm benchBoard --fresh` prints them beside the published tables above. Times by the clock are your machine's: compare the ratios between libraries, not the nanoseconds.

`pnpm benchSizeScale` reruns [Size at scale](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/size-at-scale), `pnpm benchBigApp` the generated apps and ntwine, and `pnpm benchBuildTime` [Build time](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile#build-time).

The [benchmarks' README](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/blob/main/ark/repo/bench/external/README.md) has what each suite needs installed, how each library was added to it, the versions every row was measured at and every run's results.

# Troubleshooting

> What the build reports, and how to fix it.

A build that precompiles everything is quiet. Otherwise, each problem is reported in the same shape: where it is, what the build couldn't do, why, and how to fix it.

```
src/forms.ts:14:19  type(`string <= ${limit}`) cannot be precompiled
  `limit` is a parameter of makeField (src/forms.ts:12:22); its value is known only at runtime
  Write the definition where makeField is called, with the value it passes for `limit`, so the build precompiles each call.
```

Positions are your source's, even where another plugin transpiled it first. Run [`arktype-precompile --check`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#check-an-existing-project) to see every report at once.

Where the fix is clear and the problem could throw at runtime, the build fails. Where it could still write output, as for a dependency shipping precompiled validators, a read off an import it can't resolve or a definition that throws a ParseError, the hint ends `or set allowUnsafe: true to build anyway, with a warning.` What [`allowUnsafe`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#allowunsafe) builds past may then throw at runtime. What a build with `runtime: "arktype"` leaves to arktype is always reported as a warning, since nothing fails at runtime.

## Not supported

Each of these is reported by the build, or listed here where nothing can report it. Where a program needs one, build with `runtime: "arktype"`, or leave that part dynamic.

| What | Instead |
| - | - |
| Parcel, Metro (React Native), Deno and Jest, which have no plugin or driver | Bundle with a [supported bundler](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#bundlers), and test with Vitest, `node --test` or `bun test`. For React Native, see [Frameworks](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#frameworks) |
| esbuild without `bundle: true` | Set `bundle: true` |
| `arktype` left external, as by `external`, webpack's `externals`, tsup or tsdown | Let the bundler bundle it |
| Types defined in a Svelte component or another file that isn't JS or TS | Define them in a `.ts` or `.js` module the component imports |
| Types defined in a virtual module, esbuild's `stdin`, a `data:` URL or `node --eval` | Define them in a file |
| A definition reading a value known only at runtime | Make it static, or mark it as a [runtime island](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands) |
| Composing or introspecting a Type at runtime, like `.and()` or `.json` | Compose inside a definition, or set [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) |
| Errors in a [locale](https://arktype.io/docs/i18n) other than English | A runtime island |
| A narrow or morph passing `ctx.reject()` `meta`, or `flags` without a `code` | Read `message`, `path` or `expected`, or [a runtime island](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands) |
| A dependency that defines Types but doesn't opt in | Set it in [`dependencies`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#dependencies), or have it [opt in](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#libraries) |
| A dependency that ships its own precompiled validators | Have it publish its source and opt in |
| `prune: true` outside Vite, Rollup, Rolldown, esbuild, webpack and Rspack | Leave `prune` unset |
| `declare: true` with esbuild, Bun, Farm or Node | Run `arktype-precompile --declare` after building |
| `errors: "none"` or `optimizeErrors: "size"` with `arktype-precompile --emit` | A bundler or the Node driver |

## Definitions

**`... cannot be precompiled`**: the definition reads a value known only at runtime, like a parameter or the result of a call the build can't evaluate. The hint names the value, as in ``Replace `process.env.MAX` with a value the build can read``: make it a literal or a const holding one, mark the definition as a [runtime island](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands), or build with `runtime: "arktype"`. A helper whose body is one expression, or consts, `if`s that return and a final `return`, like ``(max: number) => type(`0 < string <= ${max}`)``, precompiles at each call passing it values the build can read, like literals, consts and Types. So does one holding a Type it's passed, like `(item: Type) => type({ data: item })`. A value known only at runtime can still be passed where only a function the helper creates reads it, as `saved` is in `(saved: Address | undefined) => Address.narrow(a => a === saved || isComplete(a))`: the narrow runs as data is validated, so the build precompiles the definition once and each call passes its own function. For a parameter of another function, write the definition or the call where that function is called, with the value it passes. Where nothing calls it by name, like a callback passed to a library, mark the definition `// @ark-runtime`, as only arktype sees what it's passed.

The hint ends **`A // @ark-runtime island can't define this one alone, as what it composes is precompiled.`** where the definition composes other Types or helpers, like `type({ user: User, role: process.env.ROLE })`: an island can validate with a precompiled validator but not compose it, so marking this definition alone would fail for each one it reads. Move what varies into a narrow or morph, mark each definition it composes too, or build with `runtime: "arktype"`.

The reason **`calls a hook, whose result is known only as a component renders`** names a call like `useLocale()` in a definition a component makes as it renders. Define the Type in the module, and read what the hook returns in a narrow or morph a helper creates, as in `const fieldOf = (locale: string) => Field.narrow((data, ctx) => check(data, locale, ctx))`, called as the component renders.

**`` `text` (...) is not a static helper: it runs `let unit = ...` (...), where a static helper holds only consts, `if`s that return and a final `return` ``**: the build evaluates a helper's body at each call only when it's one expression, or consts, then `if`s whose branches return, then a final `return`, as in `if (!exists(data)) { return ctx.reject(...) } return true`. Any other statement, like a `let`, a loop, a `throw`, a const after an `if`, or an `if` that doesn't return, keeps its calls from being precompiled. Write the helper in that shape. A check of what a Type infers, like `schema.infer satisfies User`, may stand anywhere in it, since it does nothing as it runs.

**`the function at ... is created by each call to a static helper, so the precompiled site cannot reach it`**: a helper returning a function creates a new one at each call. A precompiled validator reads it off what the call returns, like `labeled("Name")` returning `{ message: ctx => ... }` in `.configure(labeled("Name"))`, or a Type the helper's own precompiled definition returns, as in `type({ name: trimmed("a name") })`. It can't where that definition reads the helper's parameter, so the build precompiles it at each call instead, or is marked `// @ark-runtime`. Declare the function in the module and pass it, as in `const message = (ctx: ArkError) => messageOf(labels, ctx)` and `.configure({ message })`.

**`` `shape` is written at ..., so its value at the site is not known ``**: the definition reads an object or array the program changes before it, through a member, a method like `push`, `Object.assign` or a function writing its argument, so the build can't tell what it holds there. Write the value whole in its literal. Where it differs by case, define a Type for each case and choose one at runtime.

**`` `Plan.limit` is 4, but was precompiled as 3 ``** or **`` `currencies` holds other keys or values than it was precompiled with ``** (thrown as a validator is created): the definition reads an object or array that code the build doesn't follow changed before the definition ran, like a module loading it with `require()` or `import()`, a dependency, or a read of `export * as`. The build refuses a definition only where it sees the write, so the validator checks each value it read as it's created. A production build checks a list or enum read whole, like `Object.values(Plan.Enum)`, by a digest, so it says only that one changed, and a development build names the key. A build written for size, as `optimize: "size"` or the `"smallest"` preset sets, leaves each name out of the bundle and says `A value a validator reads` in its place, so build with `optimize: "speed"` to read which value it was. Write the value in the definition, or don't change it after it's exported.

**Both Types of `import.meta.env.DEV ? DevPost : Post` ship**: nothing reports this. The build reads each module before the bundler replaces a constant like `import.meta.env.DEV`, so it precompiles both Types, and a production bundle written as one chunk declares the units every validator it reaches reads in [one function](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#prune), which the bundler keeps whole. It drops `DevPost` but not the checks only `DevPost` reads. Set `prune: false` to let the bundler drop those too, at the cost of what pruning saves elsewhere, or define one Type for both.

**`... can't be precompiled yet`**: the definition uses something the build doesn't support yet. Build it as a runtime island, or with `runtime: "arktype"`.

**`.default() gives the definition of an object's key, not a Type`**: `.default()` and `.optional()` return what an object's key is defined as, not a Type, so a `const` can't hold one in a standalone build. Write it at the key it's for, as the message shows: `{ plan: Tier.default("free") }` in place of `const Plan = Tier.default("free")` and `{ plan: Plan }`.

**`arktype runs this callback while defining the type`**: a callback arktype calls during definition, rather than during validation, must be a static helper the build can compute: one expression, or consts, `if`s that return and a final `return`. arktype calls a narrow as it defines a union with a unit branch, like `type("string").or(type.undefined).narrow(isSet)`, to decide that branch, and keeps it for the others, which the build precompiles the same way.

**`` `f` can run before `B` (...) is set; export `B` so the site can receive it ``**: an import cycle can reach the definition before a binding it reads is set. Export the binding.

**`... throws a ParseError`**: the definition is invalid, like an intersection that can never be satisfied, so the build fails, with `runtime: "arktype"` too. Fix the definition. Under `allowUnsafe` it's a warning, and the definition throws the same ParseError at runtime, as a test expecting one means it to.

**`` `// @ark-runtime` marks nothing ``**, **`` `const x = 1` is marked // @ark-runtime but doesn't use arktype ``** or **`... is marked // @ark-runtime inside a definition the build precompiles`**: a [runtime island](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands) marker leaves nothing to arktype. Put `// @ark-runtime` right before a definition arktype should run, or remove it. `allowUnsafe` doesn't change this.

**`schemas["..."] matches no file`**, **`... names Money, which declares no definition here`**, **`... matches ..., which holds no definition`** or **`` `// @ark-strategy` marks no definition ``**: a key of [`schemas`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#strategies-and-schemas) or a strategy marker chooses for nothing. Name the module or the top-level declaration holding the definition, as the message's `Did you mean` does where one is close, or remove it.

**`... names the strategy "...", which isn't one`**: a key or marker names a strategy the build lacks. Name `"fastest"`, `"smallest"` or one `strategies` defines.

**`schemas["..."] and schemas["..."] both match ..., and neither names more of its path`**: two globs choose different strategies for a module, and each writes as much of its path before its first wildcard. Name the module in a key of its own, or write more of its path in one of them.

**`... chooses a strategy for a definition // @ark-runtime leaves to arktype`**: arktype creates a [runtime island](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands)'s Type as the program runs, so the build writes no validator for a strategy to decide. Remove the marker or the key naming it.

## Reads

**`` `type` is used outside a precompiled site ``**: a standalone build doesn't ship arktype, so a call that creates a Type must be a definition the build precompiles. Move it into one, or build with `runtime: "arktype"`.

**`messageIn(issue, locale) calls messageIn, which arktype/runtime doesn't export`**: a standalone validator writes its messages in English, so read `issue.message`, or build with `runtime: "arktype"` to write it in a locale. `byPath`, `flatByPath`, `flatMessagesByPath` and `byAncestorPath` read a validator's errors as they read arktype's.

**`import("arktype") loads arktype, which a standalone build replaces with arktype/runtime`**: the build precompiles definitions it sees through an `import` declaration, and resolves every other load of arktype to its runtime, which can't create a Type. Import it with an `import` declaration, or build with `runtime: "arktype"`.

**`` `text` is read outside a call the build precompiles ``**: the build precompiles a helper whose definition reads its parameters at each call, so the helper itself never runs. Passed as a callback, held in an object, exported as a default or loaded with `import()`, it would be called where the build can't see the call. Call it directly, with arguments the build can read.

**`x.description reads description, which a standalone validator lacks`**: a validator lacks the methods that compose a Type. It also lacks an introspection member the program reads off it outside a definition, as through a function's parameter, unless [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) sets it, though a read like `User.description` is replaced by its value. Compose inside a definition, set the member, or build with `runtime: "arktype"`. A helper composing a Type it's passed, as `<t>(T: Type<t>) => T.or("null")` does, precompiles at each call passing it a Type the build knows, as long as its body is one expression, or consts, `if`s that return and a final `return`. Otherwise, make it a Generic, `type("<t>", "t | null")`, which the build precompiles where it's called. Composing what a call returns, as in `addressOf(saved).or("undefined")`, is a definition too, where the call returns a Type. `User.infer` and the other type-only members, `t`, `inferIn`, `inferOut` and `inferIntrospectableOut`, are `undefined` on a Type as on a validator, so `typeof User.infer.address` is never reported.

**``User.array composes `User`, which can't be precompiled``**: the build refused the definition of `User`, so nothing composing it can be precompiled either. The reasons under it are those of `User`'s own report, which is the one to fix: `Fix the definition it composes, as that one's report says, and the build precompiles this one with it.` A definition holding it, like `type({ user: User })`, ends with the same hint.

**``opts.default reads default ... the build can't tell where `opts` comes from``**: a value the build has no source for, like an exported function's parameter or a callback's, may be a Type, so reading a member a Type has and a validator lacks, like `default`, `in`, `out` or `to`, fails. Annotate the value with an interface, a type literal, a type alias of one or a type from a package other than arktype, declared in its module or imported from a relative path, as `(opts: Options) => opts.default`. The build can't read `any`, `unknown`, `object`, `typeof x` or a type computed from others, like `Parameters<typeof f>[0]`, and what's read off a member typed `unknown` or `any` is checked as an unannotated value is.

**`` `User` comes from `~/schemas`, which the build can't resolve ``**: neither TypeScript nor the bundler resolves the import to a file, as for a virtual module, so the build can't check reads off it. `--check`, the ESLint rule, Bun and the Node driver [resolve as TypeScript does alone](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/validators#what-a-validator-has), so there an import only a bundler alias resolves can't be checked either. Add the alias to `tsconfig.json`'s `paths`, or name that tsconfig as the build's `tsconfig`. If the value isn't a Type, annotate it with its type. `paths` apply to every file under the nearest `tsconfig.json`, including one its `include` leaves out, like a test beside `src`, as a bundler's alias would.

**`` packages/models/lib/index.js is CommonJS, which the build reads only where it sets `exports.Color` once, to a value, as tsc writes `export const Color = ...` ``** (under `` `Color` is an import the build cannot follow ``): the build reads a CommonJS module as tsc writes one, which is how a workspace package built ahead of the app usually reaches it: `exports.a = value`, `__exportStar(require("./a"), exports)` for `export *`, `exports.a = __importStar(require("./a"))` for `export * as a` and the getter tsc defines for `export { a } from`. It can't read an export set twice or any other way, like the `enum` tsc writes or `module.exports = { ... }`. Declare an enum as a const object, `export const Color = { Red: "red" } as const`, write its values in the definition, or point the package's `exports` at ES modules or its TypeScript source.

**`` `out.items` is read off what may be an arktype value ``**: the build lost track of what a value is somewhere between it and an arktype value, like a Module it can't read, so it may be a Type, which a validator replaces. An annotation doesn't change that. Define a Scope or Module in a const, as `scope({ ... })` or `scope({ ... }).export()`, which the build reads alias by alias, or build with `runtime: "arktype"`.

**`` `getPlaces()` may be a Scope ``** or **`it's passed to code the build can't see`**: a standalone build replaces a Scope or Generic it precompiles with an object that has none of its members, so it precompiles one only where it can see each read, including through a parameter annotated `Scope`, `Generic` or `typeof $`, an object or array literal holding it, a `let` it's assigned to or another module importing it. Assign the Scope to a const and read off that, as in `const $ = getPlaces()` and `$.type(...)`, keep it out of exported functions and functions the build can't analyze, or build with `runtime: "arktype"`.

## Setup

**`arktype resolves to 3.0.0-rc.7, but @ark/aot runs on 3.0.0-rc.8`**: validators run only on the arktype they were built with. Where your program imports the other version, as after upgrading arktype alone, the message names the `@ark/aot` released with it, e.g. `npm i -D @ark/aot@<version>`. Where it's an arktype released before `@ark/aot`, which pnpm and yarn install beside it with only a peer warning, the message names the arktype `@ark/aot` runs on, e.g. `npm i arktype@<version>`. Where a dependency does, install one version, e.g. with your package manager's dedupe or overrides.

**`precompiledForArktype_<version>` is not exported by `arktype/runtime`** (each bundler words it its own way; CommonJS emitted by `--emit` throws `This module needs arktype/runtime to export precompiledForArktype_<version>, ...` when loaded): a module of validators was linked to the runtime of another arktype version than it was [built for](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#installation), usually from a bundler cache kept from before an upgrade, a stale `--emit` build, or a second copy of arktype. Install one version, clear the bundler's cache or rebuild with `arktype-precompile --emit`. ESM `--emit` relies on static ESM imports for this version check, so post-transforming emitted ESM files file-by-file to CommonJS (e.g. Jest, Babel or SWC) skips link-time validation; emit CommonJS or bundle instead.

**`The bundle leaves arktype to be loaded at runtime`** (or `arktype/runtime`): the program would load arktype, or a second copy of its runtime, beside the runtime its validators use, so `out instanceof type.errors` would be false for their errors. A tool that leaves dependencies external does this unless told otherwise: with tsup, add `noExternal: ["arktype"]`, and with tsdown, `deps: { alwaysBundle: [/^arktype(\/|$)/] }`. Where every import of arktype's runtime is left external, as with esbuild's `packages: "external"`, the program loads one copy, and the build allows it.

**`Next.js leaves the pages router's dependencies external on the server`**: the server would then load arktype beside the runtime its validators use, so `out instanceof type.errors` would be false for their errors. Add `bundlePagesRouterDependencies: true` to the Next config, as [Next.js](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#next) shows. With webpack, the message also offers the narrower **``or add "arktype", "arkregex" to `transpilePackages`, so it bundles only those``**, which leaves every other dependency external as before. The plugin reads each module Next leaves external, so a build passing with it has no dependency loading a copy of its own, and one that does fails naming the package to add. With Turbopack, `transpilePackages` isn't enough, as the loader can't see a dependency left external loading its own copy.

**The build's `serverExternalPackages` option leaves a package** (Turbopack): the package imports arktype, and either router's server would load it, and arktype with it, beside the runtime your validators use. Remove it from `serverExternalPackages`.

**`The bundle leaves @hono/arktype-validator, which imports arktype`**: the package would load arktype from Node, beside the runtime your validators use, so `out instanceof type.errors` would be false for their errors there. With Vite on a server, add it to `ssr.noExternal`, or the option the message names for another environment. Elsewhere, bundle it: remove it from the bundler's `external` option, or, with tsup, add it to `noExternal`, and with tsdown, to `deps.alwaysBundle`. For a package defining Types, like `drizzle-arktype`, the message also names the [`dependencies`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#dependencies) setting it needs, which alone bundles it on Vite's server. The build reads the modules your imports of the package load, and assumes a computed `import()` or `require()` among them reaches arktype. It only reads a package whose manifest, or a dependency's, declares arktype, and only in a build, as [Setup](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#bundlers) says.

**The @ark/aot/turbopack loader reads `serverExternalPackages` from `next.config`**: the loader reads the list from `next.config` without running it, as running it again could start a server or write files. Write it in that file as an array of string literals.

**`arktype resolves to more than one copy`**: one copy doesn't recognize another's Types and errors. The message names each copy and the file that reached it.

**`arktype resolves to ... rather than arktype/runtime`** or **`arktype/schema/runtime resolves to ...`** (Turbopack): add the `turbopack.resolveAlias` entries the message lists to your Next config. See [Next.js](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#next).

**``configure() is called, but the build has no `config` module``**, or in a [production build](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#production-builds) **``configure() is called, but the build's `config` is false``**: name the module that calls it as the build's [`config`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#configuration) in `ark.json`, as `{ "precompile": { "config": "./src/arktype.config.ts" } }`.

**``--check can't read the `config` precompile.vite() is passed``** or **`... sets errors other than precompile.vite() at vite.config.ts:5:12`**: `arktype-precompile --check` reads the options a plugin call at the project's root passes, imported, required or loaded by `import()`, but only those written as literals, and only where every call agrees. Set the option in `ark.json`, which the plugin reads too, or pass it to `--check` as a flag.

**`... loads src/schemas.ts, which creates a Type, before the config module src/config.ts runs configure()`**: creating that Type would throw unless the program loaded the config module earlier. Import the config module first, before any module that creates a Type.

**`precompile.esbuild() needs bundle: true`**: precompiled modules import validators the bundle includes.

**`my-schemas imports arktype, which a standalone build resolves to arktype/runtime, where defining a Type throws`**: a dependency defines Types but doesn't [opt in](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#libraries). Where it defines them statically, like t3-env's `presets-arktype`, precompile it with this in `ark.json` (or `package.json`'s `"ark"` key):

```json
"precompile": { "dependencies": { "my-schemas": "aot" } }
```

A definition reading one of its Types, like `type({ email: Email })` with `Email` imported from it, is refused as `can't be precompiled yet` with the reason `` `my-schemas` is a package the build does not read, though it imports arktype `` and the same fix. Where it creates them from values it reads as it runs, like `drizzle-arktype` from your tables, set `"arktype"` in place of `"aot"` to run it on arktype. Turbopack can't, so its message (`which Turbopack resolves to arktype/runtime`) says to build with webpack or `runtime: "arktype"`. See [`dependencies`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#dependencies). Better still, have it publish its source with `"ark": { "aot": true }` in its `package.json`. `allowUnsafe` builds it anyway, but the dependency then throws where it defines a Type. A dependency reading only `type.errors` or `ArkErrors` off arktype, like `@hono/arktype-validator`, builds as it is.

**`precompile.dependencies names drizzle-arktyp, which can't be resolved from /app`**: name a package the program depends on, as its `package.json` names it.

**`drizzle-arktype runs on arktype, whose errors aren't instances of type.errors under errors: "none"`** (or `optimizeErrors: "size"`): a build writing errors of its own can't mix them with arktype's. Precompile it with `"aot"` if its Types are static, or build without that option.

**`precompile.dependencies runs drizzle-arktype on arktype, which Turbopack can't`** (or Bun's runtime plugin): it replaces arktype for every importer. Set the dependency to `"aot"` if its Types are static, or build with webpack (`next build --webpack`) or `Bun.build`, or with `runtime: "arktype"`.

**`/app/package.json sets "ark.precompile" and /app/ark.json is beside it`**: both set the build's options. Move `"precompile"` from one file to the other. `"aot"` may stay in `package.json` beside `ark.json`.

**`my-schemas imports arktype/runtime, so it ships validators precompiled for one version of arktype`**: a dependency shipped its own precompiled build, which runs only on the arktype it was built with. Have it publish its source and opt in instead, with `"ark": { "aot": true }`.

**`src/Form.svelte imports arktype, which a standalone build resolves to arktype/runtime`**: the build can't precompile a module that isn't JavaScript or TypeScript, like a Svelte component's script. Move what it reads off arktype into a `.ts` module it imports: define its Types there, and for an `instanceof type.errors` check, export a function the component calls, like `export const isInvalid = (out: unknown) => out instanceof type.errors`.

**`src/Form.svelte:4:20  User.description can't be precompiled in a module another plugin writes`** or **`src/Form.svelte:9:21  User.errors reads errors, which a standalone validator lacks`**: Vite, Rollup, Rolldown, webpack and Rspack builds read a component, a route TanStack Router splits, or a file an import names with a query (as `./schemas.ts?v=1`), as its plugins write it, but can't write a validator there, so a read only a precompiled site serves, or one a validator lacks, would read `undefined` at runtime. Move it into a module the component imports, as [Frameworks](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#frameworks) shows.

**`arktype's plugin is listed ahead of TanStack Router's`**: TanStack Router's code splitting moves a route's component into a module of its own, so arktype's plugin has to read the route after it. List `precompile.vite()` after `tanstackRouter()`, as [Frameworks](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#frameworks) shows.

**`src/fields.ts exports text, a helper the build precompiles at each call, but src/Form.svelte imports it and isn't a module the plugin transforms`** or **`... exports text, a helper the build precompiles at each call, but it's an entry`**: the build precompiles a helper whose definition reads its parameters at each call it sees, so a call it can't see, from a module it doesn't transform or from outside the bundle, would throw at runtime. Call the helper in a module the plugin transforms and import what it returns, or, from an entry, export what it returns. A Rollup, Rolldown, Vite, esbuild, webpack or Rspack build reports this; the Vite dev server, Vitest and the other drivers don't, so there it's the runtime error below.

**`virtual:schemas imports arktype ... as it can't precompile a module with no file of its own`**: the build precompiles modules from their files, so not one a plugin loads from a virtual id or namespace, esbuild's `stdin`, a `data:` URL or code given to `node --eval`. Define the Types it uses in a file it imports.

**`src/schemas.ts imports arktype ... as another plugin loaded it before precompile.esbuild() could`**: esbuild loads a module with the first plugin that returns its contents, so a plugin ahead of this one kept it from being precompiled. Put `precompile.esbuild()` ahead of that plugin.

**`must be valid according to t`**, or `$ark.t` in a morph's `toJSON()`, where the function was anonymous: terser, which webpack minifies with, can inline the call a precompiled site makes and assign your function to a variable, which names it. It renames every function anyway unless told not to, so where a message names one, give it a name and set [`keep_fnames`](https://terser.org/docs/options/#compress-options). Validation is unaffected.

**A narrow keeping state passes on Rspack where it fails elsewhere**, with or without precompiling: Rspack's minifier writes `const patterns = [/a/g]` and `s => patterns[0].test(s)` as `s => /a/g.test(s)`, a new regex at each call, so its `lastIndex` never advances. Bind the regex itself, as in `const re = /a/g`, or set `optimization.minimize` false.

**`type is not a function`** at runtime: a module that defines a Type loaded `arktype/runtime` without being precompiled. Bun's driver and Turbopack replace `arktype` for every importer, so they can't fail for a module they don't load, like one another plugin supplies or, with Turbopack, one no loader rule matches. Define the Types it uses in a file they precompile. The same error comes from a call to a helper the build precompiles at each call, made from a module the build doesn't transform: call the helper where it does.

**`toJsonSchema isn't precompiled`** warned at runtime in development, or the same for another introspection member: code the build didn't see read a member it didn't bake, like code outside the bundle reading a validator an entry exports. Set it true in [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members). The member reads `undefined`, in development as in production, so code only testing whether the validator has it goes on, and what fails is code calling it, as `toJsonSchema is not a function`. A production build warns nothing.

**`A standalone validator's JSON Schema takes only a target it was built with, and a fallback only where it was built to apply one`**: code passed `toJsonSchema()` options its baked schema can't apply. A validator takes each `target` and applies a `fallback` where it also bakes `~standard.jsonSchema`, as where a library like hono-openapi converts it, or where [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) sets `toJsonSchema`, so set it true where code the build doesn't see passes either. It still throws where arktype reads what a fallback returns other than to write a union, as for a `Date` with keys of its own or a symbol key. Build those with `runtime: "arktype"`.

**`... was written by a build whose cache kept it in ..., where it no longer is`**: delete the bundler's cache to rebuild.

**`The @ark/aot/turbopack loader can't read this project whole, because ...`**: `next build` [couldn't read your project](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#next) up front, so each module holds its own validators. The build is right, but larger and slower to load. Remove what the message names, or set `prune: false` to build so without the warning.

**`... which the @ark/aot/turbopack loader's read of the project didn't see, so a validator may lack what it reads`**: Turbopack built a module otherwise than `next build` read it, so a validator it left a member out of may be read for it. The message names the module and how it differs. Remove the difference, or set `prune: false`.

**`next build` hangs, or panics with `turbo-tasks: an internal panic occurred`, once you remove the `arktype/schema/runtime` alias** (Turbopack): Next 16.4.1 hangs a build, with its build cache on, after one that resolved an import inside a dependency through an alias it no longer has, as removing the precompiler's setup does. Delete `.next/cache` once.

**Turbopack builds a module as it did before you linked or patched arktype**: Turbopack's persistent cache keeps what the loader wrote until the module, a file it read, or the version of `arktype` or `@ark/aot` changes. A linked copy or a patch changes their code without the version, so delete `.next/cache` after changing either. The build's own cache, and webpack's and Rspack's, rebuild by themselves.

**`prune: keeping assert, meta, ~standard, methods and withContext, because the validator at src/schemas.ts:3:14 is lost where src/server.ts:12:30 passes it to send, which the build can't follow`**: a production build couldn't prove what its validators are read for, so it kept each member [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) leaves to it. The warning names the first read or module that stopped it, as [prune](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#prune) lists them. Set each member it names in `members`, false where no code reads it, like `assert` where nothing asserts, and true where a library may, like `~standard` for one taking a Standard Schema. The build then writes what you set without the warning, and still prunes what else it can. `prune: false` would build each unit as a module of its own as well, which is larger.

**`precompile: baking each introspection member into the validator at src/router.ts:9:14, because src/router.ts:24:10 passes it to t.procedure.input, which the build can't follow`**: a production build lost track of what reads a validator, so it baked each introspection member into it, as [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) describes. Set each in `members`, false where no code reads it, to build without the warning.

**`precompile: compiled to check fastest, this bundle's validators would be about 1.4 times the size of arktype, which they replace, so the build wrote them as calls to checkers they share`**: a production build of a bundle a browser loads holds so many Types, or Types so large, that the code compiled for them would outweigh arktype, so with `optimize` unset the build wrote them as [`optimize: "size"`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#choosing-smallest) does, reading the bundle a second time to. Set `optimize: "size"`, or `preset: "smallest"`, to build so without the warning and the second read, or `optimize: "speed"` to compile them.

**`precompile: this build's validators, each compiled to check fastest, are about 1.4 times the size of arktype, which they replace`**: the same, in a build that can't tell whether a browser loads its bundle, like Turbopack's or a Rollup build, so it left them compiled and the bundle is larger precompiled than it would be creating its Types as it runs. Set [`preset: "smallest"`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#choosing-smallest), which writes them as calls to checkers they share, or `optimize: "speed"` to keep them compiled without the warning. The size is an estimate from the code the build wrote, which a minifier and the chunks a bundler splits it into change, and a build reading one module at a time, as with `prune: false`, has no bundle to size, so it doesn't warn.

**`the bundle it built reads more than the modules it read: a module reads assert of a validator. Another plugin wrote or rewrote a module after it read it`**: a production build reads each module from its file to [prune](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#prune), so a module another plugin wrote or rewrote can read a member the build left out. List `precompile.vite()` right after your framework's plugin and ahead of `react()` and any Babel plugin, as [Frameworks](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#frameworks) shows, so it reads your modules as you wrote them. A plugin that adds a read of a validator, like a macro, fails the build in either order, after arktype's with the message below: set the member it reads true in [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members), or `prune: false`.

**`vite-plugin-macros transformed src/form.ts after arktype's plugin read it, and the program as built reads what the build left out of its validators: a module reads assert of a validator`** (Vite, Rollup or Rolldown): a plugin whose transform runs after arktype's added a read to a module arktype had read, which a pruned build sees only once the bundle is built. The message names each plugin whose transform follows arktype's, the module and the read. No order of plugins keeps what the read needs. Set each member the message names true in [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members), which builds what the read needs and still prunes the rest. Where it names none, as for a validator the added code passes to a function, or errors it reads off a call that no module you wrote reads, leave out the read or set `prune: false`.

**`vite-plugin-wrap changed the validators arktype's plugin wrote in src/types.ts, so the build can't check what the program as built reads of them`** (Vite, Rollup or Rolldown): a plugin whose transform runs after arktype's changed the code arktype's wrote in place of a module's definitions, as one wrapping each export does, so a pruned build can't tell what the module reads of its validators. Give the plugin `enforce: "pre"` and list it ahead of `precompile.vite()`, or with Rollup or Rolldown list it ahead of arktype's, so arktype's reads what it wrote, or set `prune: false`. One that only rewrites the code around them, as TypeScript's transform does, isn't reported.

**`built src/form.ts after arktype's loader read it, and the program as built reads what the build left out of its validators: a module reads assert of a validator`** (webpack or Rspack): a loader after arktype's added a read to a module arktype had read, as Babel does where Next's webpack build finds a Babel config. The message names each loader that ran after arktype's, and the read: a member, or errors read off a call that no module arktype read reads. Run the one adding the read ahead of arktype's, leave out the read, or set `prune: false`. Next.js orders its own loaders, so there remove the Babel config or plugin adding the read, or set `prune: false`.

**`ts-loader compiles src/form.ts to CommonJS after arktype's loader read it, so the build can't check what the program as built reads of its validators`** (webpack or Rspack): a loader after arktype's turned a module's `import`s into `require()` calls, which a pruned build can't follow. Have it emit ES modules, as TypeScript's `module: "esnext"` does, or set `prune: false`. A Vite, Rollup or Rolldown build says the same of a plugin whose transform follows arktype's. A module written as CommonJS, like a workspace package tsc built ahead of the app, isn't reported, as the build keeps each member of what it loads.

**`prune: off, because src/routes.ts:3:1 reads import.meta.glob, which may load modules it can't name`**: a production build couldn't read every module the bundle holds, so it built its validators as `prune: false` does. Set `prune: false` to build them the same without the warning.

**`prune: off, because it built src/types.ts from two codes`** (webpack or Rspack): the bundle holds one file as two modules with different code, as where a loader applies to only one of its importers, so the build can't read the program as one. Have each importer build it the same way, or set `prune: false`. The modules Next.js's `experimental.optimizePackageImports` builds a listed package's entry as aren't reported: the build reads each as the entry's file. The build is right either way, but built whole, every validator keeps each member, and one a module exports its JSON and JSON Schema too, which can make the bundle larger than one that ships arktype, so set the [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) no code reads to `false`, which `arktype-precompile --check --members '{"json":false,"toJsonSchema":false}'` checks in seconds.

**`configure() is given other values than arktype in this thread already applied`**: the config module changed while the build ran, as by an edit in watch mode, or a plugin ahead of arktype's transforms it before arktype reads it. Restart the build after an edit. Otherwise exclude the config module from the plugin the message names (Vite names it; other bundlers can't tell which): the build configures arktype from the module as written, so a plugin's rewrite of it can't take effect in either order. Behind arktype's plugin, it would leave the program configuring arktype with other values than its build's, which throws `configure() received values other than its build's` as the program starts.

**`@ark/aot's precompiler stopped before it answered`**: the precompiler runs in a worker thread, and a module the process preloads into every thread, usually through `NODE_OPTIONS`, threw there. The message names the preloads `NODE_OPTIONS` lists. Pass the module to `node` as a flag instead, as `node --import ./setup.ts`, which stays out of the precompiler's thread, or return from it early where `isMainThread` from `node:worker_threads` is false. The worker's error isn't printed, since the build stops first; the message gives a one-line `node -e` command that starts a worker under the same `NODE_OPTIONS` and prints it, with its stack.

**`No tsconfig.json is in ... or a directory above it`** (`--emit`, `--declare` or `declare: true`): create the file the message names, as `{ "compilerOptions": { "rootDir": "src", "outDir": "dist" }, "include": ["src"] }`, or name the one `tsc` builds with as `--tsconfig`, or as `"tsconfig"` in `ark.json`.

**`warning: Api is declared with any where its type refers to itself, which TypeScript can't write`** (`--declare` or `declare: true`): a [cyclic](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#cyclic-types) Type's declaration was left to TypeScript, which writes `any` where its type recurs, so code importing it gets `any` there. It's a warning, and the declarations are written. `--declare` names a cycle where a top-level `const`, default export or function infers the Type, Scope or Module, so bind one a class's member or a generic function holds to a `const` of its own, like `const types = scope({ ... }).export()`, and export a class a cyclic definition names with `instanceof`. Otherwise, annotate the declaration with a type you write.

# Advanced

> Shadow mode, libraries, runtime islands, declarations and optimizations.

## Shadow mode

`shadow: true` makes a test suite tell where a standalone build would behave otherwise than arktype. Each definition is precompiled and also created by arktype from the same values, and the program runs on arktype, only `arktype/config` resolving to the runtime:

```ts
import { precompile } from "@ark/aot/unplugin"
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config"

export default defineConfig({ plugins: [precompile.vite({ shadow: true })] })
```

Each Type, Module and `type.fn` compares its validator with arktype's as it's created, as it validates (by result, the input it leaves and each call to a function the program passed) and as its members are read. Where they agree, it returns arktype's result. Where they don't, it throws an error naming the definition, what was observed and both results, and raises it again where a fallback or `expect(...).toThrow()` can't catch it.

During a validation, each function a definition holds runs once, its calls and plain writes to its arguments replayed for the validator. A call that adds an error to `ctx` or writes otherwise, like setting a `Date`'s time, runs again for the validator, which must answer alike.

## Libraries

A library ships its definitions unprecompiled, as its source or what `tsc` emits from it, and the build precompiles them with the program if its `package.json` opts in:

```json
{
	"name": "my-schemas",
	"ark": { "aot": true }
}
```

A program can do the same for a package that doesn't opt in, with `"precompile": { "dependencies": { "my-schemas": "aot" } }` in its settings; see [`dependencies`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#dependencies). The plugin and drivers find such packages among those the nearest `package.json` to `cwd` depends on, directly or through other packages, and the plugin keeps Vite and Vitest from prebundling or externalizing them.

A library shouldn't ship what its own build precompiled, which runs only on the arktype it was built with, so the build fails for each dependency that imports `arktype/runtime`.

## Runtime islands

In a standalone build, a definition can be left to arktype by marking it:

```ts
// @ark-runtime
export const Shaped = type(await loadShape())
```

The marker applies to the statement or expression after it, and what follows it on its line is a reason the build ignores, as in `// @ark-runtime its shape is loaded`. arktype then ships beside `arktype/runtime` for the modules with islands alone. The build fails if an island reads a precompiled validator other than to validate with it, or reaches arktype outside an island, e.g. through a helper in another module. So an island suits a definition that stands alone. For one that composes other Types or calls a helper, like `type({ user: User, role: process.env.ROLE })`, the island would need each of them marked too, and the report of a definition the build can't precompile says so in place of suggesting the marker: `A // @ark-runtime island can't define this one alone, as what it composes is precompiled.` There, move what varies into a narrow or morph, which runs as data is validated, or build with `runtime: "arktype"`. It fails too for a marker that leaves nothing to arktype: one nothing follows, one on code that doesn't use arktype, or one inside a definition the build precompiles. `--check` leaves islands out of its rate.

`@ark/fast-check` reads arktype's nodes, so the build requires an island to call it, and resolves its own `arktype` imports to arktype rather than its runtime. Bun and Turbopack replace `arktype` for every importer, so with them, build a program calling it with `runtime: "arktype"`.

[`fromJsonSchema`](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/from-json-schema) is precompiled like `type` where the build can read its argument, except a JSON Schema `"object"`, which excludes arrays with a predicate of arktype's own, so it needs an island.

## Declarations

If you ship types derived from arktype, as a published package does, declare them with `--declare` rather than `tsc`, so consumers don't infer arktype definitions. For a [cyclic scope](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#cyclic-types), it's the only way to ship them:

```sh
npx @ark/aot --declare
```

It only writes declarations, so it needs no bundler, and the validators it declares can stay dynamic.

This writes what `tsc --emitDeclarationOnly` would for the nearest `tsconfig.json`, or the one `--tsconfig` names, except that each Type, Scope and Module is declared through its shape in one `~arktype.d.ts` at the declarations' root, named once and referenced wherever another shape holds it:

```ts
// users.d.ts
export declare const User: import("arktype").Type<import("./~arktype.js").User>

// ~arktype.d.ts
export type User = {
	id: string
	role: import("arktype").Default<Role, "member">
	address?: Address | undefined
}
```

A consumer's type-check then reads each Type's shape rather than inferring its definition.

It declares a Type, Scope or Module this way wherever a module's top-level declaration infers one: a `const`, each name of a destructured one, a default export, a key of an object and what a function returns. A shape TypeScript can't name where a consumer resolves it, like a class its module doesn't export, is left to TypeScript's own declaration, as are a class's members. The CLI exits with 1 where TypeScript reports an error, after writing what it emitted.

A declaration that holds a Type's data rather than the Type references the same names. `tsc` writes the shape out again wherever a library's type holds it, like the `input` of a tRPC procedure:

```ts
// router.ts
export const appRouter = t.router({
	createUser: t.procedure.input(User).mutation(({ input }) => ({
		message: `Created ${input.name}`
	}))
})

// router.d.ts, from tsc
export declare const appRouter: import("@trpc/server").TRPCBuiltRouter<
	{
		/* ... */
	},
	import("@trpc/server").TRPCDecorateCreateRouterOptions<{
		createUser: import("@trpc/server").TRPCMutationProcedure<{
			input: {
				name: string
				age: number
			}
			output: {
				message: string
			}
			meta: object
		}>
	}>
>

// router.d.ts, from --declare
export declare const appRouter: import("@trpc/server").TRPCBuiltRouter<
	{
		/* ... */
	},
	import("@trpc/server").TRPCDecorateCreateRouterOptions<{
		createUser: import("@trpc/server").TRPCMutationProcedure<{
			input: import("./~arktype.js").User
			output: {
				message: string
			}
			meta: object
		}>
	}>
>
```

A Type with a [morph](https://arktype.io/docs/intro/morphs-and-more) or a default has an input and an output that differ from its shape, so a declaration holding one names it `SignupIn` or `SignupOut` beside `Signup`. A type a library derives from a Type's, as Hono does for what `c.json` returns, isn't the Type's own and stays as TypeScript wrote it, as does a literal union or a global like `Date`.

If your tsconfig sets `declaration`, run `--declare` after `tsc`, which writes the same files. Under `isolatedDeclarations`, TypeScript reports each export without an annotation and declares none of its module, from `--declare` as from `tsc`.

### Cyclic types

TypeScript can't write a type that refers to itself unless the type has a name, and the type arktype infers for a [cyclic](https://arktype.io/docs/scopes#cyclic-types) alias has none. So for a module exporting one, `tsc` writes `any` where the type recurs, which is what code importing it gets, or, depending on its version, fails with `TS5088: The inferred type of 'types' references a type with a cyclic structure which cannot be trivially serialized` ([microsoft/TypeScript#64656](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/issues/64656)). `--declare` names each cycle for its alias in the scope:

```ts
// types.ts
export const types = scope({
	User: { name: "string", "friends?": "User[]" },
	Group: { members: "User[]", "parent?": "Group" }
}).export()

// types.d.ts
export declare const types: import("arktype").Module<
	import("./~arktype.js").types
>

// ~arktype.d.ts
export type types = {
	User: User
	Group: Group
}
export type User = {
	name: string
	friends?: User[] | undefined
}
export type Group = {
	members: User[]
	parent?: Group | undefined
}
```

A name another shape has is numbered, like `User$2` for a second scope's `User`, and a Type that recurs through [`this`](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#this) is named for its const. Code that reads a cyclic Type's data is declared with the same names, as `(data: unknown) => types.User.assert(data)` is with `User`.

Where `tsc` reports TS5088, turn `declaration` off in the tsconfig it builds your JavaScript with, since `--declare` writes the declarations.

A cycle `--declare` leaves to TypeScript is still declared with `any`. The CLI [warns of each](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/troubleshooting) without failing, as in `src/api.ts: warning: Api is declared with any where its type refers to itself`.

The bundler plugin emits the same files with a Rollup, Rolldown, Vite, webpack, Rspack or Rsbuild build that neither watches nor serves:

```ts
precompile.vite({ declare: true })
```

esbuild, Bun, Farm and the Node and Turbopack drivers can't tell whether a build watches, so `declare: true` throws there; run `npx @ark/aot --declare` after the build instead.

Declarations read your program with the TypeScript it's built with, from the optional `typescript` peer: the compiler API of TypeScript 5.5 to 6, or for TypeScript 7.1 or later, its native API, which `tsgo` serves, or [tsrs](https://www.npmjs.com/package/tsrs) where its binary is installed. `checker` (`--checker`) chooses one of `"tsjs"`, `"tsgo"` and `"tsrs"`:

```sh
npx @ark/aot --declare --checker tsgo
```

TypeScript 7 orders an object's keys and a union's members as it declares them itself, so the shapes it declares can list them in another order than 6's. `"tsjs"` in a TypeScript 7 project reads TypeScript 6 installed beside it:

```sh
npm i -D typescript-6@npm:typescript@6
```

## Equal definitions

arktype returns one Type for a scope's equal definitions written alike, and for spellings it normalizes alike. [Other spellings](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#types-are-built-when-theyre-first-read) of one Type can be two equal Types. A precompiled program compares the same, including any function a Type holds, except:

- A Type the build leaves to arktype, as a [runtime island](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands), and its precompiled equal are two values.
- A build that reads each module alone, as Node and `arktype-precompile --emit` do, and any build that doesn't [prune](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#prune), gives two values for a Type holding a cycle and for one in a scope a function creates. Reading the whole program, as a production build on Vite, Rollup, Rolldown, esbuild, webpack or Rspack does, or `next build` with Turbopack, compares them as arktype does.
- A scope a function creates is created once, however often the function is called, so each call's Types are one value where arktype creates them anew.
- A chunk imported again at runtime under another URL creates its functions anew, so arktype gives each run its own Type for a narrow the chunk defines. A validator holding a function the build proves can't differ between runs may be one value for both. A webpack or Rspack runtime keeps each module it ran and runs none again, so a build on either asks for no such proof of a function a module declares as it runs, except in a file the bundle holds as two modules, like one built in two layers. It assumes a module that ran is never run again: with `output.strictModuleErrorHandling`, a module required again after its run threw runs twice, and a validator its first run created then reads the functions of the second.

## Optimizations

What a build writes, and the [options](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options) that change it.

### Valid and invalid data

The default build writes two functions for each Type: a check returning whether data is valid, and a pass finding its issues, which a validator runs only for data the check rejects. Valid data costs only the check. For most Types without a narrow or morph, the pass runs once the errors' `issues` or `summary` is [first read](https://arktype.io/docs/errors#arkerrors), so invalid data costs little more than its check until then. A build that writes its errors for size finds them as it validates.

| Option | Saves | Costs |
| - | - | - |
| [`preset: "smallest"`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#choosing-smallest) | bytes, more the more Types a bundle holds | validation speed, and startup, creating every validator |
| [`optimizeErrors: "size"`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#optimize-and-optimizeerrors) | bytes of the issue-finding pass | time reading issues |
| [`errors: "first"`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#errors) | time on invalid data, stopping at its first issue | the other issues |
| [`errors: "none"`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#errors) | the issue-finding pass and every message | every issue but one root issue, `is invalid` |
| [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) | each member set false | reading it |
| [`jsonInput: true`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#jsoninput) | time checking objects that reject undeclared keys, by counting the keys | an undeclared key can pass on data that isn't plain |

### What nothing reads

Each Type's creation is annotated `/* @__PURE__ */`, so your bundler drops a Type nothing reads, without `sideEffects: false` in your `package.json`, unless creating it could throw.

A [production bundle](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#prune) that reads every module it holds leaves out the members no read needs, and the parts of the error runtime no validator in it writes: formatting an array index in a path, writing text configured for a code and, where no [runtime island](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/advanced#runtime-islands) runs, the message a TraversalError writes for errors arktype returns. Where no module names `TraversalError`, it leaves out the class too: `assert` throws an `Error` with the same `name`, `message` and `arkErrors`, which is all a program that can't test `instanceof TraversalError` reads of one. Where only a module it doesn't read, like a dependency, imports the class, the class ships and `assert` throws an instance of it. Written as one chunk, it also declares the units its validators share in one function.

### Large modules on Turbopack

Where `next build` [can't read its project whole](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/setup#next), each module holds its own validators, so it can't write a program's code once. A route would spend its first request on Types it may never call, so a module writing a lot of code creates each validator's checks at its first call rather than as the module loads. A validator is still there from the import, with its identity and members, and what a Type reads from your code is read and checked on import, so nothing about when a guard fires changes. The cost is a few more instructions per call to read the check through a variable.

[`lazy: false`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#lazy) and `optimize: "size"` leave a module as it is.

### Unions

A union of objects is checked by one key where a key tells its branches apart. Among keys at the shallowest path, ArkType prefers one every branch holds, then the one with the most values. A branch without the key is checked in every case, and data matching no case reports through it as well as the key, so give each branch the key:

```ts
// one switch on kind: { kind: "c" } fails with kind must be "a" or "b"
const Event = type.or(
	{ kind: "'a'", x: "number" },
	{ kind: "'b'", y: "string" }
)
```

### Minifiers

A default build writes each Type's checks as small functions calling each other, which V8 inlines as it runs them. terser, webpack's default minifier, and swc, Next.js's, write a function called once into its caller, as a closure created at each call or a module variable, either of which runs slower. So the build annotates each such call `/* @__NOINLINE__ */`, which both honor and every minifier drops from its output. Minified by either, validators run as fast as unminified, and the functions they keep cost some bytes, most in a large app minified by swc. esbuild and oxc don't inline them. A build for size calls the runtime's checkers instead, and writes no annotation.

Rolldown, which Vite 8 bundles with, keeps only `@__PURE__`, `@__NO_SIDE_EFFECTS__` and `@vite-ignore` comments, so a terser pass after it never sees the annotations. A Vite build with `build.minify: "terser"` inlines the functions, so its validators run slower. Keep Vite's default minifier, oxc, or use esbuild:

```ts
import { precompile } from "@ark/aot/unplugin"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({
	plugins: [precompile.vite()],
	build: { minify: "oxc" }
})
```
